q: A strategic proposal called for first occupying Jing and Yi Provinces, allying with Sun Quan, waiting for a change in the situation in the north, and then advancing along two routes. If Jing Province were lost, which key precondition of this strategy would no longer hold?
reply:
**Short answer: the precondition that fails is 「跨有荊、益」 — holding Jing and Yi together — and with it the Jingzhou half of the two-route advance.**

The proposal is Zhuge Liang's reply to Liu Bei, recorded in his biography:

「若跨有荊、益，保其巖阻，西和諸戎，南撫夷越，外結好孫權，內修政理；天下有變，則命一上將將荊州之軍以向宛、洛，將軍身率益州之眾出於秦川」[1]

In English: if you cross over and hold Jing and Yi, secure their fastnesses, befriend the western Rong and pacify the southern Yi and Yue, outwardly knit good relations with Sun Quan, inwardly order government — then when there is a change in the empire, order one senior general to lead the Jingzhou army toward Wan and Luo, while the general himself leads the Yi province host out through Qin Chuan.

The ally-and-wait clauses (「外結好孫權」, 「天下有變」) are conditions for action; the action itself is a two-pronged pincer, with the Jingzhou army as one arm and the Yi province army as the other. The territorial precondition stated for the whole plan is 「跨有荊、益」.

So if Jing were lost, the clause that no longer holds is the joint possession of Jing and Yi; concretely, the Jingzhou army's march toward Wan and Luo could no longer be mounted, leaving only the Yi province prong out through Qin Chuan. The alliance with Sun Quan and the timing condition are separate clauses and are not by themselves what Jing's loss removes — the text ties the two-route advance to 「跨有荊、益」.

This last part is an inference from the wording of the passage, not a separate statement in the record: the plan as written assigns one of its two attacking arms to Jingzhou's army, so without Jingzhou that arm cannot be fielded.

q: Cao Cao took in Emperor Xian of Han and issued orders in the name of the Han central government. Compared with relying on military strength alone, what political advantage did this chiefly bring him?
reply:
The chief political advantage was legitimacy: by holding the emperor, Cao Cao could turn his own commands into the Han court's commands, so that rivals were put in the position of disobeying the dynasty rather than merely resisting a warlord. The sources put this in terms of "using the Son of Heaven to command those who will not submit," and of winning the allegiance of the realm's talent.

The clearest statement is Mao Jie's advice to Cao Cao at Yanzhou: 「夫兵義者勝，守位以財，宜奉天子以令不臣，脩耕植，畜軍資，如此則霸王之業可成也。」[11] Xun Yu's argument in Jian'an 1 is the fuller version: 「誠因此時，奉主上以從民望，大順也；秉至公以服雄傑，大略也；扶弘義以致英俊，大德也。」[5] — that is, following the people's hopes, overawing the powerful, and drawing able men. Cao Cao acted on it: 「太祖遂至洛陽，奉迎天子都許。」[5]

That this was felt as a genuine political asset, not just a formality, is shown by how others reasoned about it. Jia Xu urged Zhang Xiu to submit to Cao Cao on precisely this ground: 「夫曹公奉天子以令天下，其宜從一也。」[21] The Fu Zi commentary likewise says: 「是時，太祖奉天子以號令天下，方招懷英雄以明大信」[18] — so the emperor's name was also what let Cao Cao present himself as trustworthy and thus attract heroes. Cao Cao himself told Jia Xu: 「使我信重於天下者，子也。」[21] Conversely, Yuan Shao's recorded reaction is the same coin from the other side: 「曹操當死數矣，我輒救存之，今乃背恩，挾天子以令我乎！」[3] — from this one can infer that it was the imperial sanction attaching to Cao Cao's orders that made them hard for a man like Yuan Shao to shrug off, since he frames the grievance as Cao Cao "holding the Son of Heaven" to order him about.

A further point follows from the records: control of the court also let Cao Cao rebuild the machinery of state: 「自天子西遷，朝廷日亂，至是宗廟社稷制度始立。」[8] And the authority in question came from the emperor's own grant rather than from Cao Cao's troops alone — 「天子拜太祖大將軍」, with later titles conferred the same way [5][8][10]. So the advantage was, in the sources' own framing, that military force won battles while the Han court's name won submission, recognition, and recruits; that the two worked together, and which mattered more in a given case, is a judgment the texts do not settle for us.

q: One side had the advantage in troops and supplies; the other, in a prolonged standoff, was running short of grain. In the end the weaker side, acting on intelligence from a defector, raided the enemy's main grain depot and turned the battle around. Which battle was this, and who was the defector?
reply:
This was the Battle of Guandu (官渡之戰), fought in Jian'an 5 = 200, between Cao Cao and Yuan Shao, and the defector was Xu You (許攸), a strategist in Yuan Shao's camp.

Yuan Shao had by far the larger force; Pei Songzhi, noting the disparity, quotes the Benji: 「紹衆十餘萬，屯營東西數十里」[13]. Cao Cao's side was the one short of supplies: 「公與紹相拒連月，雖比戰斬將，然衆少糧盡，士卒疲乏」[12]. Ju Shou had summed up the asymmetry to Yuan Shao earlier: 「北兵數衆而果勁不及南，南穀虛少而貨財不及北；南利在於急戰，北利在於緩搏」[11].

The intelligence came from Xu You, described in the Wudi ji as 「紹謀臣許攸貪財，紹不能足，來奔，因說公擊瓊等」[12]. The Xun Yu biography gives the immediate motive: 「審配以許攸家不法，收其妻子，攸怒叛紹」[5]. The Xun You biography has him report the target's weakness: 「會許攸來降，言紹遣淳于瓊等將萬餘兵迎運糧，將驕卒惰，可要撃也」[4].

Cao Cao then struck the depot at Wucao, which lay forty li from Yuan Shao's camp (「瓊宿烏巢，去紹軍四十里」[11]). He went himself with 5,000 horse and foot: 「太祖乃留曹洪守，自將步騎五千候夜潛往攻瓊」, and 「破瓊等，悉斬之」[11]; the Wudi ji says 「大破瓊等，皆斬之」[12]. Pei Songzhi's note quotes the Cao Man Zhuan for how it was done — the raiders marched under Yuan banners (「皆用袁軍旗幟」) and 「盡燔其糧穀寶貨」[1]. The same note preserves Xu You's own advice to Cao Cao: 「今袁氏輜重有萬餘乘，在故市、烏巢，屯軍無嚴備；今以輕兵襲之，不意而至，燔其積聚，不過三日，袁氏自敗也」[1]. With the grain burned, the army broke: 「紹衆大潰，紹及譚棄軍走，渡河」[12].

One discrepancy should be flagged rather than smoothed over. The Zhang He biography has Yuan Shao's army already collapsing and Zhang He surrendering for fear of Guo Tu's slander, whereas Pei Songzhi notes that the Wudi ji and the Yuan Shao tradition instead have Zhang He and Gao Lan surrender upon hearing Wucao had fallen, which is what caused the rout: 「至如此傳，爲紹軍先潰，懼郭圖之譖，然後歸太祖，爲參錯不同矣」[10]. The sources agree on the essentials — Guandu, Xu You's defection, the raid on the grain — but not on the exact sequence of Zhang He's surrender.

q: This man originally served under Liu Zhang but later became one of Liu Bei's key advisers. He helped plan the seizure of Yi Province and accompanied Liu Bei in the contest for Hanzhong. He died of illness before Liu Bei did, and so had no part in the deathbed entrustment. Who was he?
reply:
That man was **Fa Zheng (法正), courtesy name Xiaozhi (孝直)** of Fufeng Mei — someone Liu Bei, in Zhuge Liang's own words, "always loved and trusted" (「先主雅愛信正」[20]).

**His start under Liu Zhang.** Fa Zheng entered Shu with Meng Da in the early Jian'an years and served Liu Zhang as magistrate of Xindu, then as military adviser (軍議校尉), but felt unused: 「既不任用，又為其州邑俱僑客者所謗無行，志意不得」[1]. He befriended Zhang Song, who judged Liu Zhang unable to accomplish anything: 「益州別駕張松與正相善，忖璋不足與有為」[1].

**Planning the seizure of Yi Province.** When Liu Zhang feared Cao Cao's move on Hanzhong, Zhang Song recommended Fa Zheng as envoy to Liu Bei, and Fa Zheng secretly gave Liu Bei the plan: 「以明將軍之英才，乘劉牧之懦弱；張松，州之股肱，以響應於內；然後資益州之殷富，馮天府之險阻，以此成業，猶反掌也」[1]. So Liu Zhang sent him with 4,000 men to welcome Liu Bei, "and Fa Zheng took the occasion to set out the plan for taking Yi Province" (「遣法正將四千人迎先主，前後賂遺以巨億計。正因陳益州可取之策」[6]). After the conquest he was made Administrator of Shu Commandery and "the chief strategist within" (「外統都畿，內為謀主」[20]).

**Hanzhong.** In Jian'an 22 he urged Liu Bei to strike: with Cao Cao's forces withdrawn, Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He could be beaten [11]. Liu Bei approved, "and Fa Zheng accompanied the march" (「先主善其策，乃率諸將進兵漢中，正亦從行」[11]). In Jian'an 24, at Dingjun Mountain, it was Fa Zheng who said "we can attack now" (「正曰：『可擊矣。』」), whereupon Liu Bei ordered Huang Zhong to charge and Xiahou Yuan was killed [11]. Cao Cao's remark on hearing of it: 「吾故知玄德不辦有此，必為人所教也」[11]. During the campaign, when Liu Bei refused to retreat under a rain of arrows, Fa Zheng stood in front of him, and Liu Bei yielded: 「孝直，吾與汝俱去」[21] (Pei Songzhi's commentary).

**Death and the deathbed scene.** When Liu Bei became King of Hanzhong, Fa Zheng was made Prefect of the Masters of Writing and General of the Guard; "the following year he died, aged forty-five. The Former Lord wept for him for days" — 「明年卒，時年四十五。先主為之流涕者累日」, posthumous title Yi Hou [4]. Since Liu Bei became King of Hanzhong in Jian'an 24 and Fa Zheng died the next year, while Liu Bei himself died at Yong'an (Baidi) in Zhangwu 3 [23], Fa Zheng clearly died first — from this it follows that he could not have been present at the deathbed entrustment. Zhuge Liang later sighed: 「法孝直若在，則能制主上，令不東行；就復東行，必不傾危矣」[4]. He was also the only man given a posthumous title during Liu Bei's lifetime: 「先主時，惟法正見諡」[25].

Chen Shou's verdict: 「法正著見成敗，有奇畫策算，然不以德素稱也」, comparing him to Cheng Yu and Guo Jia [26].

q: This man first served Yüan Shao and later went over to Ts'ao Ts'ao. He fought in Han-chung, defeated Ma Su at Chieh-t'ing, and finally died at Mu-men while pursuing the Shu army. Who was he?
reply:
The man was **Zhang He (張郃)**, courtesy name Junyi (雋乂), of Mo county in Hejian. All the clues match his biography in the *Wei Shu*.

**From Yuan Shao to Cao Cao.** He first served Han Fu, then "以兵歸袁紹" [4] — he brought his troops over to Yuan Shao, who made him a Colonel and sent him against Gongsun Zan. At Guandu he advised Yuan Shao to rescue Chunyu Qiong at Wuchao; when his advice was not taken and the army collapsed, Guo Tu slandered him, and "郃懼，乃歸太祖" [4] — out of fear he went over to Cao Cao (Taizu). Cao Cao received him gladly, comparing him to "微子去殷、韓信歸漢" [9]. Note that the sources differ on the sequence: Pei Songzhi points out that the *Wudi ji* and *Yuan Shao zhuan* say Zhang He and Gao Lan surrendered first and Yuan Shao's army then collapsed, whereas this biography says the army collapsed first and Zhang He surrendered out of fear of Guo Tu's slander — "爲參錯不同矣" [11].

**Hanzhong.** After Zhang Lu surrendered, Cao Cao "留郃與夏侯淵等守漢中，拒劉備" [9]. He took Badong and Baxi, was checked by Zhang Fei at Dangqu ("爲備將張飛所拒，引還南鄭" [9]), and after Xiahou Yuan's death the officers pushed him forward as commander: "遂推郃爲軍主" [14].

**Jieting.** When Zhuge Liang came out to Qishan, Zhang He was sent to resist Ma Su: "拒亮將馬謖於街亭。謖依阻南山，不下據城。郃絶其汲道，擊，大破之" [16]. The Shu side records the same defeat: "與魏將張郃戰於街亭，為郃所破" [2].

**Death at Mumen.** Pursuing Zhuge Liang's withdrawing army, "郃追至木門，與亮軍交戰，飛矢中郃右膝，薨，諡曰壯侯" [1]. The *Houzhu zhuan* places the same event slightly differently: "郃追至青封，與亮交戰，被箭死" [7]. Pei Songzhi's note quotes the *Weilü* that Sima Xuan-wang (Sima Yi) ordered the pursuit over Zhang He's objection — "軍法，圍城必開出路，歸軍勿追" — and that Zhang He, forced to advance, was hit by arrows from an ambush [5]. Whether this note or the main text reflects the actual course is left as two versions; the *Weilü* says the arrow struck his thigh (髀), while the main text says the right knee (右膝).

q: Before the Battle of Red Cliffs, Liu Bei was comparatively weak, while Sun Quan held the Jiangdong territory and a navy. Given this imbalance, why did Sun Quan still have an incentive to ally with Liu Bei rather than stand by and let Cao Cao destroy him?
reply:
**Short answer:** In Jiangdong's own calculation, Liu Bei was not a helpless bystander to be sacrificed — he was the asset that could keep Cao Cao from owning the whole Yangtze. Letting Cao Cao finish Liu Bei off would not have bought Sun Quan safety; it would have handed Cao Cao the river and left Sun Quan facing him alone. The alliance was not charity, it was the instrument of resistance.

**Liu Bei still had real forces, and a name that could rally Jing province.** When Lu Su first proposed the mission after Liu Biao's death, he argued that Jing was 「此帝王之資也」 [19] and that Liu Bei, 「天下梟雄，與操有隙」 [19], was the man to hold it together: 「及說備使撫表眾，同心一意，共治曹操，備必喜而從命」 [19]. He also warned against delay — 「今不速往，恐為操所先」 [19]. Zhuge Liang's own tally to Sun Quan was that Liu Bei still had Guan Yu's water force and Liu Qi's Jiangxia troops, 「今戰士還者及關羽水軍精甲萬人，劉琦合江夏戰士亦不下萬人」 [3]. So the "weak" Liu Bei brought soldiers, a claim on Jing province, and a reputation that could make Cao Cao's newly acquired Jing subjects unreliable.

**The alliance multiplied Cao Cao's enemies without costing Sun Quan command.** After the victory, when Lü Fan urged Sun Quan to detain Liu Bei, Lu Su objected that Sun Quan had just arrived in Jing and 「恩信未洽」, so he should lend the ground to Liu Bei and let him pacify it — 「多操之敵，而自為樹黨，計之上也」 [14]. That is the core incentive: Liu Bei was a buffer and a co-belligerent, useful precisely because he was not strong enough to dominate Sun Quan. Sun Quan himself put it plainly to Zhuge Liang: 「非劉豫州莫可以當曹操者」 [3].

**Surrender was not a live option for Sun Quan personally.** Lu Su's private argument is the clearest statement of why standing by was suicidal: 「今肅可迎操耳，如將軍，不可也」 — a subject like Lu Su could surrender and still get a minor post, but 「將軍迎操，欲安所歸？」 [17]. Zhou Yu had made the same point back in 建安七年, over Cao Cao's demand for a hostage: send one, and 「命召不得不往，便見制於人也」, ending at best with a marquis's seal instead of 「南面稱孤」 [35]. If Cao Cao destroyed Liu Bei, by this reasoning Sun Quan would be next in line with no rival left to share the pressure.

**And the Yangtze was no longer a shield by itself.** The dissenters at Sun Quan's council said the quiet part out loud: the only thing that let Sun Quan resist Cao Cao was the Yangtze — 「且將軍大勢可以拒操者，長江也」 — but 「今操得荊州，奄有其地」, having taken Liu Biao's 「蒙沖鬥艦，乃以千數」 and floated them downriver, so 「此為長江之險，已與我共之矣」, and on raw numbers 「又不可論」 [20]. With the river shared, Jiangdong needed land forces and a Jing foothold; Liu Bei supplied both. Zhuge Liang framed the payoff as 「操軍破，必北還，如此則荊、吳之勢彊，鼎足之形成矣」 [2].

**On who deserves the credit:** Chen Shou's biography of Zhou Yu presents Zhou Yu as the one who brushed aside the council and spoke for resistance; Pei Songzhi notes the biography never mentions Lu Su's prior plan, 「殆為攘肅之善也」 [36], and Pei Songzhi's own verdict is 「建計拒曹公，實始魯肅」 [21]. Pei Songzhi also flags that the Shu and Wu accounts each claim the initiative for their own man — 「各記所聞，競欲稱揚本國容美，各取其功」 [5]. So the texts disagree on authorship of the idea, not on the logic: the alliance was Jiangdong's own best move.

**What the sources record as the debate:** the council discussion is between迎降 and fighting, with Liu Bei as the means of fighting [17][20][2]. There is no recorded deliberation about standing aside while Cao Cao destroyed Liu Bei first — that scenario is not among the options the text puts before Sun Quan.

q: This man did not personally lead the army that conquered Shu, yet he pushed the war of conquest forward while he controlled the Cao-Wei court. His son later replaced Cao-Wei and founded the Western Jin. Who was he?
reply:
That man was **Sima Zhao (司马昭)**, known in the sources as 司马文王 / 晋文王, father of **Sima Yan (司马炎)**, who took the throne from Cao-Wei and founded the Jin dynasty.

**He directed the conquest of Shu without leading the armies himself.** The *Sanguozhi* account of Zhong Hui records that it was Sima Zhao who decided on the campaign and assigned the commands: 「文王以蜀大將姜維屢擾邊陲，料蜀國小民疲，資力單竭，欲大舉圖蜀」, and 「景元三年冬，以會為鎮西將軍、假節都督關中諸軍事」; in the autumn of Jingyuan 4 (= 263 CE) he issued the edict sending Deng Ai and Zhuge Xu with over 30,000 men each, while 「會統十餘萬眾，分從斜谷、駱谷入」 [2]. The Deng Ai biography states it plainly: 「四年秋，詔諸軍征蜀，大將軍司馬文王皆指授節度」 [6] — Sima Zhao, as General-in-Chief, personally gave all the instructions and dispositions. He did not march with the invading army; when he finally moved west, it was to Chang'an to deal with the aftermath of Zhong Hui's revolt, as he himself said: 「我到長安，則自了矣」 [1].

**His son replaced Cao-Wei.** In the fifth month of Xianxi 2 (= 265 CE) the Wei court granted him the regalia of a Son of Heaven and raised his heir from 世子 to 太子; then 「秋八月辛卯，相國晉王薨。壬辰，晉太子炎紹封襲位，總攝百揆」 — Sima Zhao died in the eighth month, and Sima Yan inherited his position and took over the whole government [21]. In the twelfth month of that same year the last Wei emperor abdicated: 「天祿永終，歷數在晉。詔羣公卿士具儀設壇于南郊，使使者奉皇帝璽綬冊，禪位于晉嗣王，如漢魏故事」 [32].

So the man you are looking for is Sima Zhao: the actual field commanders of the Shu campaign were Deng Ai and Zhong Hui, but the war was pushed forward by Sima Zhao, who controlled the Wei court, and his son Sima Yan then took the throne and founded the Jin dynasty.

q: The Oath of the Peach Garden: after Liu Pei, Kuan Yü and Chang Fei swore brotherhood, what was the order of seniority among the three?
reply:
The famous "Oath of the Peach Garden" itself is not recorded in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*: what the text records is that Liu Bei treated Guan Yu and Zhang Fei with the affection of brothers, and — important for the order of seniority — that Guan Yu was the older of the two by several years, and Zhang Fei served him as an elder brother.

The clearest statement is in Zhang Fei's biography: 「張飛字益德，涿郡人也，少與關羽俱事先主。羽年長數歲，飛兄事之。」[2] — "Zhang Fei, styled Yide, a man of Zhuo commandery, as a youth together with Guan Yu served the Former Lord. Guan Yu was several years older; Zhang Fei served him as an elder brother."

Guan Yu's biography describes the bond among the three: 「先主與二人寢則同床，恩若兄弟。」[1] — "The Former Lord slept in the same bed with the two men, their affection like that of brothers."

So from what the *Records* say: Liu Bei stands first, and between the other two Guan Yu was older and Zhang Fei younger, with Zhang Fei deferring to Guan Yu as his elder brother. That gives the order Liu Bei — Guan Yu — Zhang Fei.

Two caveats. First, the *Records* records no peach-garden ceremony, no oath, and no formal sworn brotherhood — 「恩若兄弟」[1] ("affection like brothers") describes their closeness, not a ritual pact; the peach-garden oath belongs to later tradition. Second, the text explicitly ranks Guan Yu above Zhang Fei (「羽年長數歲，飛兄事之」[2]), but it never states that Liu Bei was the eldest of the three by age; placing Liu Bei first is an inference from his being the lord whom the other two 「俱事先主」[2] ("together served the Former Lord"), not a recorded birth order.

q: While Kuan Yü was attacking Fan in the north, Sun Ch'üan's side seized Chiang-ling and other places in his rear. Why could Kuan Yü still collapse so quickly overall, even though he had won a major victory on the northern front?
reply:
Short answer: his northern "victory" was the destruction of Yu Jin's relief army, not the taking of Fan; while he was still pinned in front of an untaken city, his rear was taken almost without a fight — the two commanders holding Jiangling and Gong'an surrendered at once, Lü Meng had hidden his move and then used Guan Yu's own soldiers' families to kill their will to fight, and Guan Yu was left with no line of retreat and no help. The collapse was not a battlefield defeat but the loss of his base, his stores and his army's morale.

**The northern front was never finished.** In the 24th year of Jian'an (219 AD, per the era conversion) Guan Yu attacked Cao Ren at Fan: 「是歲，羽率眾攻曹仁於樊」[2]. Autumn rains flooded the Han River, Yu Jin's seven armies were drowned, Yu Jin surrendered and Guan Yu cut down General Pang De — 「秋，大霖雨，漢水汎溢，禁所督七軍皆沒。禁降羽，羽又斬將軍龐德」[2] — so that 「羽威震華夏」[2]. But the city was not taken; Sun Quan's biography states plainly 「惟城未拔」[42], and Cao Cao sent Xu Huang: 「而曹公遣徐晃救曹仁，羽不能克，引軍退還」[2].

**His own rear commanders were disaffected and surrendered at once.** Mi Fang, administrator of Nan commandery, was at Jiangling and Shi Ren at Gong'an: 「又南郡太守麋芳在江陵，將軍士仁屯公安，素皆嫌羽輕己。羽之出軍，芳、仁供給軍資，不悉相救。羽言『還當治之』，芳、仁咸懷懼不安。於是權陰誘芳、仁，芳、仁使人迎權」[2]. When Lü Meng arrived, 「士仁、麋芳皆降」[15]. These were the places that held Guan Yu's people and property: Lü Meng 「盡得羽及將士家屬」, and 「羽府藏財寶，皆封閉以待權至」[15]. They changed hands without a siege.

**Sun Quan's side planned it and hid the move.** Lü Meng memorialized that Guan Yu kept reserve troops behind precisely for fear of him — 「羽討樊而多留備兵，必恐蒙圖其後故也」[15] — so he asked to be recalled on the pretext of illness and 「遂稱病篤」; 「羽果信之，稍撤兵以赴樊」[15]. He then went upriver with picked men hidden in the holds, 「使白衣搖櫓，作商賈人服」, seized Guan Yu's river watch posts, 「是故羽不聞知」[15]. Lu Xun, newly posted to Lukou, sent Guan Yu a flatteringly humble letter, after which 「羽覽遜書，有謙下自托之意，意大安，無復所嫌」[36]; Lu Xun then took Yidu and was appointed its administrator, and that year, the 11th month of Jian'an 24, the prefectural chiefs and native leaders all surrendered [36]; Sun Quan's biography records 「陸遜別取宜都，獲秭歸、枝江、夷道，還屯夷陵，守峽口以備蜀」[42]. Sun Quan himself had written to Cao Cao asking to attack Guan Yu to prove himself: 「權內憚羽，外欲以為己功，箋與曹公，乞以討羽自效」[42]. Guan Yu, short of grain, had also 「託以糧乏，擅取湘關米」[15].

**His army dissolved rather than fought.** When Guan Yu turned back, Lü Meng treated his envoys well and let them tour the city and carry letters home: 「蒙輒厚遇其使，周遊城中，家家致問，或手書示信」, so that 「咸知家門無恙，見待過於平時，故羽吏士無鬬心」[20]. Then 「羽軍遂散」[2]; he fled to Maicheng, and 「權先使朱然、潘璋斷其徑路」, so that in the 12th month Pan Zhang's commandant Ma Zhong 「獲羽及其子平、都督趙累等於章鄉」[42], which Pan Zhang's own biography also records [37].

**No help came from the north-west.** When Guan Yu called on Liu Feng and Meng Da for troops, 「封、達辭以山郡初附，未可動搖，不承羽命」[22].

Putting this together — this part is inference from the above — the speed is explained by the fact that his power rested on the Jiangling–Gong'an base, its stores, and the families living there: the base surrendered without a siege, the stores were sealed for Sun Quan, and the soldiers learned their households were safe and better treated than before. Meanwhile the troops he had kept behind had been pulled north to Fan [15] and Liu Feng and Meng Da refused to send any [21]. His own character is also recorded as a factor: 「羽善待卒伍而驕於士大夫」[30], and Chen Shou's verdict, 「然羽剛而自矜，飛暴而無恩，以短取敗，理數之常也」[33]. The decisive mechanism in the sources, however, is that the rear changed hands without resistance and the army lost its will to fight.

q: Shu-Han's main base was Yi Province, and its northern expeditions had to haul grain across the mountains to the front. Why did 'winning a battle at the front' not necessarily mean 'being able to hold the newly gained territory for long'?
reply:
**Short answer:** Because the army that won at the front was fed by grain hauled over the Qinling mountains from Yi Province, and the newly won ground lay on the far side of those mountains. To *hold* a district you must garrison it, and a garrison must eat every day; Wei, sitting on the plains, could simply refuse battle and wait until Shu-Han's supply ran out. A victory therefore bought ground only until the next convoy failed.

The records repeatedly end a campaign with the same phrase. At Chen Cang: 「曹真拒之，亮糧盡而還」[4]; at Qishan in the ninth year of Jianxing: 「以木牛運，糧盡退軍」[2]; Jiang Wei at Nan'an: 「維糧盡退還」[21]. When Zhuge Liang moved to Wuzhangyuan in the twelfth year of Jianxing he had to try feeding the army locally: 「亮每患糧不繼，使己志不申，是以分兵屯田，為久駐之基」[2]. The transport itself was done by troops through the valleys — Zhuge Liang's letter to his brother puts Zhuge Qiao on the road: 「今使喬督五六百兵，與諸子弟傳於谷中」[11]. During the Hanzhong crisis Yang Hong put the whole province to work: 「男子當戰，女子當運」[30]. And Li Yan, charged with the rear, was ruined precisely by a failed convoy: 「值天霖雨，運糧不繼」[28].

Wei's counter-plan was to do nothing. The Mingdi edict is explicit: 「但堅壁拒守以挫其鋒，彼進不得志，退無與戰，乆停則糧盡，虜略無所獲，則必走矣」[42]. Zhang He, summoned to relieve Chen Cang, made the same calculation: 「郃知亮縣軍無穀，不能久攻」, and said 「屈指計亮糧不至十日」[38]. Pei's note quoting the *Wei Shu* shows Wei's court already assumed this: 「議者以爲亮軍無輜重，糧必不繼，不擊自破」[7].

Why the ground could not be kept. In the sixth year of Jianxing three commanderies defected to Zhuge Liang: 「南安、天水、安定三郡叛魏應亮，關中響震」[35]. But once Zhang He broke Ma Su at Jieting, the same three are recorded as retaken: 「南安、天水、安定郡反應亮，郃皆破平之」[38]; Cao Zhen likewise 「三郡皆平」[3]. A defection is not a garrison. Zhuge Liang's own response was to take the population and leave: 「亮拔西縣千余家，還于漢中」[35] — Jiang Wei does the same later, 「拔河間狄道、臨洮三縣民還」[21], and brings the surrendered Hu back with him to settle them, 「胡王治無戴等舉部落降，維將還安處之」[19]. From this pattern one can infer that Shu-Han treated newly exposed territory as something to strip of people rather than to defend, because defending it meant feeding a garrison that could only be fed from Shu.

The *Yuanzi* makes the same point from the other side: asked why Zhuge Liang did not rush to exploit the three commanderies' revolt, it answers 「蜀兵輕銳，良將少」 and that he advanced slowly out of caution [15]. Shu-Han was a small state — the *Yuanzi* elsewhere puts Zhuge Liang's force at 「戰士不滿五萬」[43] — so it could not both hold a long front and keep a field army supplied.

So the inference is: a Shu-Han victory at the front was usually won by a concentrated army at the end of a long, thin supply line. The moment that army dispersed into garrisons, each garrison had to be fed over the same mountains, while Wei could mass and counterattack from its own base. Wei's strategy of refusing battle was designed exactly to convert Shu's logistics into its defeat, and the record shows it working.

One caution: the sources do not say Shu-Han was *never* able to hold gains — it did keep Wudu and Yinping after the seventh year of Jianxing [4]. The pattern is that gains near the mountains could be held, gains out on the plains could not.

q: A Cao-Wei emperor left Luoyang to pay respects at the imperial tombs, and a senior minister who had long pleaded illness seized the chance to take control of the capital and force the other regent to surrender his power. What event was this, and who set it in motion?
reply:
This was the coup of the first month of Jiaping 1 (249 CE), the incident the histories call the Gaopingling affair (高平陵之變). It was set in motion by Sima Yi (司馬懿, posthumously Sima Xuan-wang 司馬宣王), then Grand Tutor (太傅), who had been feigning illness while Cao Shuang (曹爽), the Grand General and his fellow regent, monopolized power.

The emperor was the young Qi Prince (齊王), who had been installed when Mingdi died: 「明帝崩，齊王即位」[2]. The court record reads: 「嘉平元年春正月甲午，車駕謁高平陵」[1] — in the spring, first month of Jiaping 1, on the jiawu day, the imperial carriage went to pay respects at Gaopingling. Jiaping 1 = 249 CE, the same year as Zhengshi 10.

Sima Yi's feigned illness comes from Cao Shuang's biography: when Li Sheng was leaving to become Inspector of Jing Province and came to take his leave, 「宣王稱疾困篤，示以羸形。勝不能覺，謂之信然」[4] — Sima Yi claimed to be gravely ill and showed a wasted appearance; Li Sheng could not detect the ruse and believed it true. The background is that after Ding Mi and others persuaded Cao Shuang to keep power in his own hands, 「宣王遂稱疾避爽」[6], and 「宣王密爲之備」[6] — Sima Yi secretly made preparations.

With Cao Shuang and his brothers all accompanying the emperor to the tomb, Sima Yi struck: 「十年正月，車駕朝高平陵，爽兄弟皆從。宣王部勒兵馬，先據武庫，遂出屯洛水浮橋」[4] — he deployed troops, seized the arsenal first, then camped at the floating bridge on the Luo River, and memorialized through the Empress Dowager (「奏永寧宮」[4]) to strip Cao Shuang and his brothers of office; her order was 「皇太後令勑臣如奏施行」[4], and Cao Shuang was dismissed 「以侯就第」[1].

Huan Fan (桓範) got out of the city and urged Cao Shuang to take the emperor to Xu Chang and summon outside troops: 「範說爽使車駕幸許昌，招外兵」[8]. According to the Pei note quoting the Shiyu, Sima Yi sent Xu Yun and Chen Tai to explain matters to Cao Shuang, Jiang Ji also wrote conveying Sima Yi's intent, and Yin Damu, whom Cao Shuang trusted, told him it was only a matter of losing office, swearing by the Luo River: 「唯免官而已，以洛水爲誓」[16]. Cao Shuang gave up: 「爽於是遣允、泰詣宣王，歸罪請死」[8]. He and his party were then executed and their three clans wiped out: 「於是收爽、羲、訓、晏、颺、謐、軌、勝、範、當等，皆伏誅，夷三族」[12].

So the event was the Gaopingling coup of 249, and the man who set it in motion was Sima Yi, who used the emperor's absence at the tombs to seize the capital and force Cao Shuang, the other regent, to surrender his power.

q: Changban: who rescued the infant A'dou at Changban Slope? And who stood on Changban Bridge and scared off Cao Cao's army with his shouts?
reply:
At Changban (當陽長阪), the child was saved by **Zhao Yun (趙雲, courtesy name Zilong)**, and the man who held the riverbank and broke the bridge against Cao Cao's pursuers was **Zhang Fei (張飛, courtesy name Yide)**.

**Zhao Yun and the infant**

The Zhao Yun biography records that when Liu Bei was chased by Cao Cao at Changban and fled south abandoning his family:

「及先主為曹公所追於當陽長阪，棄妻子南走，雲身抱弱子，即後主也，保護甘夫人，即後主母也，皆得免難。」[1]

So the "weak child" (弱子) he carried in his arms was the Later Ruler (後主) — the man whose biography opens 「後主諱禪，字公嗣，先主子也」[10], i.e. Liu Shan — and Zhao Yun also protected Lady Gan, the child's mother; both escaped harm. The Later Ruler's later edict praising him says of Changban: 「當陽之役，義貫金石，忠以衛上」[2]. A passage from the *Yun Biezhuan* (《雲別傳》) adds that while Liu Bei was fleeing, someone claimed Zhao Yun had gone north to defect, and Liu Bei threw a hand-halberd at him, saying:

「子龍不棄我走也。」[3]

Zhao Yun arrived shortly after.

**Zhang Fei at the bridge**

The Zhang Fei biography says that when Liu Bei heard Cao Cao had arrived suddenly, he abandoned his family and fled, ordering Zhang Fei to bring up the rear with twenty horsemen:

「飛據水斷橋，瞋目橫矛曰：『身是張益德也，可來共決死！』敵皆無敢近者，故遂得免。」[12]

Note that the record has him holding the waterline and cutting the bridge (據水斷橋), not literally standing on the bridge — the bridge was broken behind him. As for the shouting: the text does not say his shouts drove off Cao Cao's whole army; it says he glared, leveled his spear and declared "I am Zhang Yide — come and fight to the death!", and none of the enemy dared come near, which is how Liu Bei got away. That much is the record; reading the shout itself as the cause of the enemy's retreat goes a step beyond the wording.

The main Xianzhu zhuan confirms the scene as a whole: 「先主棄妻子，與諸葛亮、張飛、趙雲等數十騎走」[7] — Liu Bei fled with Zhuge Liang, Zhang Fei, Zhao Yun and a few dozen riders, while Cao Cao captured his people and baggage.

q: Identify the stratagem: Wang Yun used Diaochan to sow suspicion between Dong Zhuo and Lü Bu, and in the end had Dong Zhuo killed by Lü Bu's hand. What is this stratagem usually called?
reply:
The stratagem is usually called the **连环计** ("chain stratagem") — it is also commonly classed as a 美人计 ("beauty trap") or a 离间计 ("estrangement plot"). But the name and the Diaochan figure belong to later tradition (the novel and opera), not to Chen Shou's *Sanguozhi*: in the *Sanguozhi* the word 貂蝉 occurs only as 貂蟬內侍, describing an attendant's headdress in the *Wei Yao* (韋曜) biography, and there is no such person as Diaochan and no arranged "chain" at all.

What the record does say is that Lü Bu's unease grew out of two things. First the halberd: 「嘗小失意，拔手戟擲布。布拳捷避之，為卓顧謝，卓意亦解。由是陰怨卓。」[8] — Dong Zhuo once threw a hand-halberd at him in a fit of temper, and from then on Lü Bu secretly resented him. Then the affair: 「卓常使布守中閤，布與卓侍婢私通，恐事發覺，心不自安。」[8] — Lü Bu carried on an illicit affair with Dong Zhuo's serving maid and, fearing discovery, felt uneasy. The maid is not named, and the text records no scheme of using her.

The actual plot is a straightforward conspiracy between Wang Yun, Shisun Rui and Lü Bu, with Lü Bu as the inside man: 「時允與僕射士孫瑞密謀誅卓，是以告布使為內應。布曰：『奈如父子何！』允曰：『君自姓呂，本非骨肉。今憂死不暇，何謂父子？』布遂許之，手刃刺卓。」[1] The *Dong Zhuo* chapter records the killing itself: 「三年四月，司徒王允、尚書僕射士孫瑞、卓將呂布共謀誅卓。」[2] and 「布曰『有詔』，遂殺卓，夷三族。」[2]

So: Wang Yun, Shisun Rui and Lü Bu plotted the killing together, and Lü Bu personally killed Dong Zhuo — that much is in the *Sanguozhi*. The romantic device of Diaochan, the betrothal-then-gift that sets the two men at odds, and the label 连环计 are not in Chen Shou's text.

q: Identify the person: when Cao Cao was routed at Wancheng, who held the camp gate and fought to the death to cover Cao Cao's retreat?
reply:
The man was **Dian Wei (典韦)**.

It is told in the *Wei Shu* biography of Dian Wei. When Cao Cao marched south, reached Wan and Zhang Xiu came out to surrender, Zhang Xiu revolted more than ten days later and raided Cao Cao's camp: 「後十餘日，繡反，襲太祖營，太祖出戰不利，輕騎引去。韋戰於門中，賊不得入。」[2] ("More than ten days later Zhang Xiu revolted and raided the Grand Progenitor's camp; the Grand Progenitor came out to fight, was unsuccessful, and withdrew with light cavalry. Dian Wei fought in the gateway, and the rebels could not get in.")

The last stand itself: 「時韋校尚有十餘人，皆殊死戰，無不一當十。賊前後至稍多，韋以長戟左右擊之，一叉入，輒十餘矛摧。左右死傷者略盡。韋被數十創，短兵接戰，賊前搏之。韋雙挾兩賊擊殺之，餘賊不敢前。韋復前突賊，殺數人，創重發，瞋目大罵而死。」[2] ("At that time Dian Wei's unit still had more than ten men, all of whom fought to the death, each one worth ten. As the rebels came up in growing numbers, Dian Wei struck left and right with his long halberd; at every thrust more than ten spears were broken. Those around him were nearly all killed or wounded. Dian Wei had received dozens of wounds and fought hand-to-hand; the rebels pressed forward to grapple him. Dian Wei seized two rebels, one under each arm, and killed them, and the rest did not dare advance. He again charged forward at the rebels and killed several; his wounds burst open, and glaring with rage he cursed aloud and died.")

The same biography records Cao Cao's response: 「太祖退住舞陰，聞韋死，為流涕，募間取其喪，親自臨哭之，遣歸葬襄邑，拜子滿為郎中。車駕每過，常祠以中牢。太祖思韋，拜滿為司馬，引自近。」[2] ("The Grand Progenitor withdrew and stayed at Wuyin; hearing that Dian Wei had died, he wept for him, had his body recovered by a side road, mourned him in person, and sent him home for burial at Xiangyi, and appointed his son Dian Man a 郎中 … Later, remembering Dian Wei, he appointed Dian Man a 司馬 and kept him close.")

The *Wudi ji* records the same defeat in the second year of Jian'an, with Zhang Xiu surrendering and then revolting: 「二年春正月，公到宛。張繡降，旣而悔之，復反。公與戰，軍敗，爲流矢所中，長子昂、弟子安民遇害。公乃引兵還舞陰」[3] ("In the first month of spring of the second year, the Duke reached Wan. Zhang Xiu surrendered, then regretted it and revolted again. The Duke fought him; the army was defeated, he was hit by a stray arrow, and his eldest son Ang and his 弟子 Anmin were killed. The Duke then led his troops back to Wuyin.") The holding of the gate and the death in battle, however, are narrated in Dian Wei's biography.

q: Sequence of episodes: put the following in the order in which they occur in *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*: A. The Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage  B. The Battle of Guandu  C. The Oath of the Peach Garden  D. The Battle of Red Cliffs
reply:
**Order:** C (Peach Garden) → B (Guandu) → A (Three Visits) → D (Red Cliffs).

The historical chronology supports this sequence. The bond among Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei belongs to the earliest stage of Liu Bei's career: Chen Shou records that 「先主與二人寢則同床，恩若兄弟」, and that Zhang Fei 「少與關羽俱事先主」[1][2]. Guandu is dated 建安五年 = 200 CE [era]. The three visits fall the year before Liu Bei's 建安十三年 defeat: Pei Songzhi infers 「備始與亮相遇，在敗軍之前一年時也」[25], i.e. 207 [era], and Red Cliffs is 建安十三年 = 208 [era].

A caveat on the first item: the Peach Garden oath itself is not in the *Sanguozhi*. What Chen Shou records of the three men's bond is only that they slept on the same bed and were 「恩若兄弟」[1] — no garden, no oath. So B, A, and D rest on the histories; the sworn-brother scene in a garden is a later, novelistic elaboration, though it is placed earliest.

**B — Guandu (200 CE).** The *Wei shu* chronicle has Cao Cao and Yuan Shao facing off at Guandu, with the night raid on the grain depot at Wuchao: 「太祖乃留曹洪守，自將步騎五千候夜潛往攻瓊」[06-0020], and 「遂以奇兵襲紹別屯，斬其將淳于瓊等，紹退走」[18].

**A — Three Visits (207 CE).** The *Zhuge Liang zhuan*: 「由是先主遂詣亮，凡三往，乃見」[23]. Pei Songzhi dates the first meeting by inference: 「備始與亮相遇，在敗軍之前一年時也」[25].

**D — Red Cliffs (208 CE).** Liu Bei 「遣諸葛亮自結於孫權」, and 「權遣周瑜、程普等水軍數萬，與先主并力，與曹公戰於赤壁，大破之，焚其舟船」[36]. Huang Gai proposed the fire attack: 「觀操軍船艦，首尾相接，可燒而走也」[32].

So: the Peach Garden bond (novelistic, placed at the outset) → Guandu (200) → Three Visits (207) → Red Cliffs (208). Note that on the three visits Pei Songzhi records a rival account from the *Weilue* in which Zhuge Liang went to see Liu Bei first, which Pei rejects as inconsistent with Zhuge Liang's own memorial [26][22].

q: Borrowing Arrows with Straw Boats: what weather conditions did Zhuge Liang take advantage of when he borrowed the arrows, and why did those conditions help him carry out the plan?
reply:
**Short answer: the fog belongs to the novel, not to the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*. In Chen Shou's text the arrow-receiving episode is Sun Quan's, not Zhuge Liang's, and no fog appears in it; the weather actually recorded around the Ruxu standoff is rising spring water and long rain.**

The arrow episode is Sun Quan's, and it is recorded without any fog. Pei Songzhi's note to the *Wu Shu* biography of Sun Quan quotes two accounts of the Ruxu campaign. The *Wei Lüe* (裴注引《魏略》) says:

「權乘大船來觀軍，公使弓弩亂發，箭著其船，船偏重將覆，權因回船，復以一面受箭，箭均船平，乃還。」[16]

So the recorded version has Sun Quan sailing a large ship to observe Cao Cao's camp, Cao Cao's crossbows firing at it, the arrows making the ship list so it was about to capsize, and Sun Quan turning the ship around to take arrows on the other side until it was level again. The *Wu Li* (裴注引《吳歷》) tells of the same visit but says Cao Cao ordered his troops not to shoot: 「敕軍中皆精嚴，弓弩不得妄發」[16]. Neither account mentions fog, straw bundles, or Zhuge Liang — the arrows are shot at the ship itself, and it is Sun Quan who receives them.

The weather that does appear in these records is water, not fog. In the *Wu Li*, Sun Quan's letter to Cao Cao reads: 「春水方生，公宜速去」[16], after which Cao Cao withdrew: 「曹公語諸將曰：『孫權不欺孤。』乃徹軍還。」[16] In Zang Ba's biography, describing the same Ruxu fighting, we read: 「行遇霖雨，大軍先及，水遂長，賊船稍進，將士皆不安」[29]. So the river conditions recorded for this campaign were spring flooding and continuous rain, and the rising water is what let the enemy's boats push forward.

As for Zhuge Liang and arrows: his biography records his devices, not any borrowing of arrows — 「亮性長於巧思，損益連弩，木牛流馬，皆出其意」[1]. The straw-boat trick with fog, in which Zhuge Liang tricks Cao Cao's archers into filling decoy boats, is the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* version. There the fog is what makes the trick work, since the archers cannot see that the targets are decoys; but no such fog, and no such trick, appears in the passages I found in the *Records*.

On why the water conditions mattered: 由此看，据《吳歷》所记孙权以「春水方生」劝曹操速去、曹操随即退军，以及《臧霸传》所记霖雨水涨而「賊船稍進」，可以推断，江水上涨有利于水军一方，而不利于从北方南下、不习水战的军队；不过这几条记载只写了水涨和船只推进，并没有明说胜负与水势的因果，这一层是推断。

q: The chained ships: before the Battle of Red Cliffs, who advised Ts'ao Ts'ao to link his warships together with iron chains? Why did this arrangement magnify the damage done by the fire attack?
reply:
**Short answer:** The histories of the Three Kingdoms do not name anyone who advised Cao Cao to chain his warships together — no such adviser appears in the surviving text. What the record does say is that Wu's Huang Gai observed that Cao Cao's warships were already "joined bow to stern," and on that basis proposed burning them. The well-known story of Pang Tong presenting a "chain stratagem" to Cao Cao is not found in these records.

**What the record actually says**

In the *Zhou Yu* biography, the initiative comes from Huang Gai, a subordinate of Zhou Yu, who reads the enemy fleet as an opportunity:

「瑜部將黃蓋曰：『今寇眾我寡，難與持久。然觀操軍船艦，首尾相接，可燒而走也。』」[2]

("Zhou Yu's subordinate Huang Gai said: 'Now the enemy is many and we are few, hard to hold out long. But I observe Cao's warships, bow to stern joined together — they can be burned and driven off.'")

The *Huang Gai* biography confirms he was the one who proposed the fire attack, and points back to the Zhou Yu account:

「建安中，隨周瑜拒曹公於赤壁，建策火攻，語在〈瑜傳〉。」[11]

So the text states that the ships were joined ("首尾相接"), and that it was Huang Gai who devised the fire attack — but it says nothing about who ordered or advised the linking. The *Jiang Biao Zhuan* note [13] and the *Shanyang Gong Zaiji* note [3] likewise only describe the burning and the retreat via Huarong, never the origin of the linking. So the adviser's identity is simply not recorded; if you have seen Pang Tong named in this connection, that is not in these histories.

**Why the linking magnified the fire**

The record makes the mechanism clear enough, though the causal wording is my inference from the accounts:

- The ships were fastened bow-to-stern into what amounted to a single mass: 「操軍船艦，首尾相接」[2]. Joined vessels cannot scatter individually — a fire started on one spreads along the line instead of being cut away.
- Huang Gai's fireships were packed with dry reeds and firewood soaked in oil: 「實以薪草，膏油灌其中」[2]; the *Jiang Biao Zhuan* adds fish-oil and notes the strong southeast wind 「時東南風急」, with the fires lit simultaneously, 「同時發火，火烈風猛」[13].
- The result was that the fire ran through the whole northern fleet and then onto land: 「燒盡北船，延及岸邊營柴」[13]; the main text says the wind 「悉延燒岸上營落」[2], and that many men and horses drowned or burned [2].

Putting these together, the point is that because the ships were bound together, the burning vessels could not be separated and towed clear, so one ignition cascaded down the line and from the ships to the shore camps. Cao Cao's army had withdrawn and camped north of the river (「引次江北」[2]), with a hard southeast wind blowing and the fleet massed together; against free-sailing ships that could disperse, the same fire would have done far less damage. That is an inference from the recorded facts — the linked formation, the oil-laden fireships, the wind, and the spread to the shore — not something the text spells out as a lesson.

q: Huarong Trail: in the novel, why does Guan Yu let Cao Cao go at Huarong Trail? What conflict within his character does this episode bring out?
reply:
**Short answer:** the Huarong Trail episode — Guan Yu blocking Cao Cao's retreat and deliberately letting him go — is not in《三国志》or in Pei Songzhi's notes. It is the novel's invention, built on materials that《三国志》does record: Guan Yu's real debt of gratitude to Cao Cao from 建安五年, and Cao Cao's own decision to let Guan Yu go. The inner conflict the novel dramatizes is the one Chen Shou names — 义, personal honor and gratitude, pulling against duty.

**What the histories actually say about the retreat.** The only account of the Huarong road is a Pei note quoting《山陽公載記》: 「公船艦爲備所燒，引軍從華容道步歸，遇泥濘，道不通，天又大風，悉使羸兵負草填之，騎乃得過。羸兵爲人馬所蹈藉，陷泥中，死者甚衆。軍旣得出，公大喜，諸將問之，公曰：『劉備，吾儔也。但得計少晚；向使早放火，吾徒無類矣。』備尋亦放火而無所及。」[4] So the man pursuing Cao Cao on that road was Liu Bei, who tried to set fire to him and arrived too late — there is no ambush and no Guan Yu. 《先主傳》and《周瑜傳》say only that the allies pursued to 南郡 and that Cao Cao turned north [1][7].

**The materials the novel drew on.** In 建安五年 Cao Cao took Guan Yu prisoner and treated him well; Guan Yu told Zhang Liao: 「吾極知曹公待我厚，然吾受劉將軍厚恩，誓以共死，不可背之。吾終不留，吾要當立效以報曹公乃去。」[15] He killed Yan Liang at Baima, then sealed up all the gifts, sent a letter of farewell and returned to Liu Bei. Cao Cao forbade pursuit: 「彼各爲其主，勿追也。」[15] Pei Songzhi also preserves a《蜀記》story that at a hunt in Xu, Guan Yu urged Liu Bei to kill Cao Cao and Liu Bei refused; later, stranded at 夏口, Guan Yu angrily reminded him of it, and Pei Songzhi argues the refusal was a matter of calculation rather than mercy [17]. So the histories contain both a debt owed to Cao Cao and Guan Yu's own record of wanting him dead. 由此看, the novel's dilemma — private gratitude (欠曹操的情) against his lord's cause and the strategic prize of killing Cao Cao — is a dramatization built on these two recorded strands, not on any recorded event; whether Guan Yu ever stood on the Huarong road, and whether he chose to let Cao Cao pass, has no basis in the histories I searched.

**The conflict within the character.** Chen Shou's appraisal names exactly this: 「羽報效曹公，飛義釋嚴顏，並有國士之風」and「然羽剛而自矜，飛暴而無恩，以短取敗，理數之常也」[11]. Repaying Cao Cao and releasing an enemy out of 义 are praised as the marks of a 國士; Guan Yu's rigidity and self-regard are named as the flaw that ruined him. The novel's Huarong scene works by putting those two sides of the same man in direct opposition — the 义 that makes him repay a kindness against the duty that should make him kill his lord's enemy.

q: Empty Fort Strategy: in the novel, where does Zhuge Liang use the Empty Fort Strategy, and which Wei commander leads the army that comes against him?
reply:
The story of the "empty fort" is told of Zhuge Liang against **Sima Yi** — but in the version that survives in the *Sanguozhi* material the place is **Yangping (陽平, in Hanzhong)**, not any place named Xicheng, and Pei Songzhi rejects the story as chronologically impossible. I have only the *Sanguozhi* and its commentary to work from, not the novel itself, so what follows is the recorded version of the episode the novel draws on.

The episode comes from Guo Chong's *Sanshi*, quoted in Pei Songzhi's note to the Zhuge Liang biography (so it is not Chen Shou's main text): 「亮屯于陽平，遣魏延諸軍並兵東下，亮惟留萬人守城。晉宣帝率二十萬眾拒亮，而與延軍錯道，徑至前，當亮六十里所，偵候白宣帝說亮在城中兵少力弱」[34]; and then 「亮意氣自若，敕軍中皆臥旗息鼓，不得妄出菴幔，又令大開四城門，埽地卻洒。宣帝常謂亮持重，而猥見勢弱，疑其有伏兵，於是引軍北趣山」[34]. The same passage has Zhuge Liang afterwards say of him 「司馬懿必謂吾怯，將有彊伏，循山走矣」[34]. So in this version: Yangping, 10,000 men kept, and the Wei commander is Sima Yi (styled 晉宣帝 / 宣帝 by his later title).

The main text of the biography records that campaign quite differently — the Wei commanders are Cao Zhen and Zhang He: 「使趙雲、鄧芝為疑軍，據箕谷，魏大將軍曹真舉眾拒之」[3], and 「亮使馬謖督諸軍在前，與郃戰于街亭。謖違亮節度，舉動失宜，大為張郃所破」[3]. The closest thing in the records to an "empty camp" trick belongs to another man and another battle: Zhao Yun, who after going out to meet Huang Zhong and being pressed by Cao Cao's army, 「雲入營，更大開門，偃旗息鼓。公軍疑雲有伏兵，引去」[20], earning Liu Bei's 「子龍一身都是膽也」[20] — and even this is from the *Yun Biezhuan* quoted in Pei's note, not Chen Shou's main text.

Pei Songzhi's own rebuttal of the Guo Chong story is explicit: 「案陽平在漢中。亮初屯陽平，宣帝尚為荊州都督，鎮宛城，至曹真死後，始與亮於關中相抗禦耳」[34]; 「此之前後，無復有於陽平交兵事」[34]; 「就如沖言，宣帝既舉二十萬眾，已知亮兵少力弱，若疑其有伏兵，正可設防持重，何至便走乎？」[34]. That is, by Pei's reckoning Sima Yi was not yet facing Zhuge Liang in the field during the Yangping stay, and a commander who had brought 200,000 men and knew his opponent was weak had no reason to bolt.

From this it follows — this part is inference, resting on the two passages above — that the "empty fort" scene as such is not in Chen Shou's main text: the only version in the material is Guo Chong's, it is placed at Yangping rather than anywhere called Xicheng, and it is doubted by Pei Songzhi. What the records do support is the Jieting defeat itself [3], with Cao Zhen and Zhang He on the Wei side; the empty-fort anecdote and its attribution to Sima Yi are a separate, contested tradition.

q: Identify the posthumous ruse: in the saying 'a dead Zhuge frightens off a living Zhongda', who is 'Zhongda'? In the novel, how does the Shu army make him retreat?
reply:
**"Zhongda" is Sima Yi.** 仲達 was the courtesy name of 司馬懿 (Sima Yi), the man the sources also call 司馬宣王 (King Xuan of Sima) and, after his posthumous honour, 晉宣王 / 晉宣帝. The saying comes from a popular proverb recorded in Pei Songzhi's commentary, quoting Xi Zuochi's 《漢晉春秋》:

「楊儀等整軍而出，百姓奔告宣王，宣王追焉。姜維令儀反旗鳴鼓，若將向宣王者，宣王乃退，不敢偪。於是儀結陳而去，入谷然後發喪。宣王之退也，百姓為之諺曰：『死諸葛走生仲達。』」[1]

("Yang Yi and the others formed up their army and marched out; the common people ran to tell King Xuan, who pursued. Jiang Wei ordered Yang Yi to turn the banners about and beat the drums, as if about to attack King Xuan; King Xuan then withdrew, not daring to press close. So Yang Yi formed ranks and left, only holding the mourning after entering the valley. When King Xuan withdrew, the people made a proverb of it: 'A dead Zhuge puts a living Zhongda to flight.'")

Sima Yi's own retort is preserved in the same note: 「吾能料生，不便料死也」[1] — "I can reckon with the living, but not with the dead."

So the saying itself is not fiction: it is a proverb quoted from 《漢晉春秋》 in Pei Songzhi's note to the Zhuge Liang chapter [1].

**What the histories record as the ruse is the flags and drums, not a wooden image.** The device that turned Sima Yi back, according to this account, was Jiang Wei's order to Yang Yi: 「姜維令儀反旗鳴鼓，若將向宣王者，宣王乃退，不敢偪」[1]. Chen Shou's own text likewise says only that Sima Yi declined to engage: 「司馬宣王與亮相持，連圍積日，亮數挑戰，宣王堅壘不應。會亮卒，其軍退還」[12]. In the material I can consult — the 《三国志》 text and Pei's notes — I find no carved wooden likeness of Zhuge Liang; the retreat-with-flags-and-drums episode is what stands behind the proverb. The statue scene belongs to the novel's expansion of this episode.

One related line, which is from Chen Shou's main text rather than a note: after the Shu army had withdrawn, Sima Yi walked over the ground of Zhuge Liang's camps and said 「天下奇才也！」[17] — "A genius of the world!" From this and the note's account of his refusal to close in on an enemy whose death he could not confirm, one can infer that his caution was not merely superstition about a dead man; but that is inference, not something either passage states.

q: Arrange 'county, province, commandery' from highest to lowest according to the usual local administrative hierarchy of the late Eastern Han.
reply:
**From highest to lowest: province (州, zhōu) → commandery (郡, jùn) → county (縣, xiàn).**

That is the usual late-Eastern Han layering, and the *Sanguozhi* shows it in the way offices are described as stacked on one another. The clearest statement is Chen Shou's comment on the Inspectors: 「自漢季以来，刺史總統諸郡，賦政于外，非若曩時司察之而已」[2] — "from the late Han on, the Inspector (刺史) commanded all the commanderies and exercised government abroad, no longer merely supervising them as before." So the province-level officer stands above the commanderies.

Below the commandery sits the county. In Xiahou Xuan's argument the county magistrates are described as already having two layers piled above them: 「今之長吏，皆君吏民，橫重以郡守，累以刺史」[27] — the long officials of today already rule over officials and people, and on top of them a commandery Administrator is piled, and above that an Inspector. He proposes abolishing the commandery so that counties report directly upward: 「若省郡守，縣皆徑達，事不擁隔」[6]. Both passages presuppose 刺史 > 郡守 > 縣.

The same nesting appears in ordinary administrative language: the commandery's officers 「職監諸縣」[6] (their job is to oversee the counties), the commandery "receives what the county has accomplished" (「郡受縣成」[6]), and new regulations are issued 「下州郡」 and then reach the 縣 (「所領六縣」[17]). Commandery Administrators and county magistrates are paired together as 「郡守百里」[23], the "hundred-li" county office being the lower of the two.

A caveat worth keeping in mind: the province (州) began in the Han as a supervisory circuit rather than a formal tier of local government. In his reply to Xiahou Xuan, Sima Yi notes that in Qin there were no Inspectors, only commandery Administrators, while the Han Inspector merely "held the six articles" and had no fixed seat: 「秦時無刺史，但有郡守長吏。漢家雖有刺史，奉六條而已」[11]. From this it can be inferred that only over the late Han did the province become the top rung of the administrative ladder above commandery and county — which is exactly why the hierarchy above is described as the late-Han arrangement.

q: In the late Eastern Han, was a 'Grand Administrator' (taishou) normally the chief official of a province, a commandery or a county?
reply:
A Grand Administrator (太守 *taishou*, also called 郡守) was the chief official of a **commandery** (郡) — not of a province (州) and not of a county (縣). In the administrative ladder as the *Sanguozhi* describes it, the province (刺史, often 州牧) stood above the commandery, and the commandery above the county (令/長).

The clearest statement comes from Jia Kui 賈逵: 「州本以御史出監諸郡，以六条詔書察長吏二千石已下」[26] — the province was originally a censor sent out to oversee the commanderies, inspecting with the Six-Article Edict the long officials of the 2000-bushel rank and below. The 太守 was exactly such a "2000-bushel" officer: Chen Shou, listing a run of 太守, calls them 「咸为良二千石」[18].

Xiahou Xuan 夏侯玄, arguing that the middle tier should be abolished, gives the same ladder: the 長吏 already rule the officials and people, yet 「橫重以郡守，累以刺史」[22] — a 郡守 is piled on above them, and a 刺史 on top of that. From this it can be inferred that the 長吏 at the bottom are the county-level heads, since he proposes 「制使萬戶之縣名之郡守，五千以上名之都尉，千戶以下令長如故」[12]: a ten-thousand-household county would be styled 郡守, and counties of a thousand households or fewer keep their 令/長 as before. He adds that if the 郡守 were done away with, 「縣皆徑達」[12] — the counties would report directly, i.e. the commandery sat between province and county.

The biographies show the office's charge is a single commandery. Wang Guan 王觀, as 太守, refuses to have his commandery underrated: 「豈可為太守之私而負一郡之民乎？」[13] — how could I, for a Grand Administrator's private interest, wrong the people of a whole commandery. You Chu 游楚, as 隴西太守, calls holding his city 「為一郡守義」[17]. Pei Qian 裴潛, sent as 代郡太守, deals with the 單于 who 「專制郡事」[1] — monopolize the affairs of the commandery.

So: province — 刺史/州牧; commandery — 太守/郡守; county — 令 or 長. The 太守 was the commandery's chief.

q: Both the 'Inspector' (cishi) and the 'Governor' (zhoumu) were offices tied to the province. What was the Inspector's original main function? And why can't every Inspector of the late Eastern Han simply be regarded as an official with supervisory powers only?
reply:
**The Inspector's original job was surveillance, not government.** The clearest statement in the *Sanguozhi* is Sima Yi's reply to Xiahou Xuan: 「秦時無刺史，但有郡守長吏。漢家雖有刺史，奉六條而已，故刺史稱傳車，其吏言從事，居無常治，吏不成臣，其後轉更爲官司耳」[20]. So the Han Inspector was a man in a relay carriage who circulated with the "six articles" (六條), had no fixed seat of government, and whose subordinates (從事) were not his "subjects" (吏不成臣). Jia Kui says the same: 「州本以御史出監諸郡，以六条詔書察長吏二千石已下」[21] — the province was originally an inspectorate sent out from the Censorate to check commandery officials of 2000 shi and below. Du Shu likewise calls the ancient Inspector one who 「奉宣六條，以清静为名，威风著称」, and asks that Inspectors be forbidden to command troops so they may attend solely to civil matters [19] — which by itself shows that in Du Shu's own day Inspectors did command troops.

**Why a late-Han Inspector cannot automatically be treated as a mere supervisor:**

1. **The office had already turned into a real territorial administration.** Sima Yi notes the change: 刺史 "afterwards gradually became a regular office (官司)" [20]. By the eve of the coalition we find Inspectors being killed by their own provinces: 「并州殺刺史張壹，涼州殺刺史耿鄙」[3]; the 涼州刺史 成就 had Dong Zhuo 「領兵騎討捕，大破之」[29]; Sun Jian 「前領豫州刺史，驅走董卓」[22]. When the coalition rose in 190, its members include 冀州牧韓馥 and 豫州刺史孔伷、兗州刺史劉岱 side by side as territorial warlords [24]. In Wei times Wang Ji was 「都督豫州諸軍事，領豫州刺史」[28] — military command attached to the inspectorate.

2. **The 州牧 was created precisely to give the province a governing, not a supervising, head.** Liu Yan proposed: 「刺史、太守，貨賂為官，割剝百姓，以致離叛。可選清名重臣以為牧伯，鎮安方夏」[12]. The "牧伯" was to 鎮安 — to pacify and hold the province; that reads as a governing and military charge, not an inspection. His plan was carried out when he himself went out 「為監軍使者，領益州牧」[3], and men like 劉虞、劉焉、賈琮 were selected from 列卿尚書 as 牧伯 [1]. The result is described bluntly in a Pei note quoting the *Yizhou Qijiu Zhuan*: 「州之牧伯猶七國之諸侯也」[16].

So the two offices differ in rank and in nature: the Inspector began as a roving inspector with the six articles and no fixed seat; the 州牧 was a high-ranking governor-general meant to hold and pacify a province. And in the late Eastern Han, many Inspectors — whether by appointment, by self-assertion, or by acquiring troops — were already acting as provincial lords, which is why 刺史 and 州牧 in that period cannot all be read as "supervisors only."

One caution on the sources: for Liu Yan, Chen Shou's text says he went out 領益州牧 [3], and the *Xu Han Shu* likewise says 劉焉為益州牧, while the *Han Lingdi Ji* says the emperor 「敕焉為益州刺史」[1] — the two accounts use different titles, and Pei Songzhi himself corrects the *Xu Han Shu*'s grouping of Liu Biao (裴松之按: 孫堅殺荊州刺史王叡，然後劉表為荊州) [1]. The title changes of this period were fluid enough that the sources do not always agree.

q: Chu-ko Liang was Chancellor of Shu-Han and also held the charge of 'Recorder of the Imperial Secretariat' (lu shangshu shi). Taking part in and overseeing what kind of business did that charge chiefly mean?
reply:
In Shu-Han the charge of *lu shangshu shi* (錄尚書事) meant overseeing the business of the Imperial Secretariat (尚書臺) — above all the handling of state documents: the receiving and issuing of imperial commands, and the flow of memorials, reports and administrative correspondence. In itself it was a secretariat charge, not a field command — that last contrast is my inference from the way the term is used below.

The Secretariat's core function is described in Wang Su's memorial, which traces it back to the ancient office of 納言: 「然後惟龍爲納言，猶今尚書也，以出內帝命而已」[17] — "then only Long held the post of 納言, which is like today's 尚書; he merely issued and received the emperor's commands."

A Wei edict quoted in the *Weilüe* shows what "overseeing" the Secretariat meant in practice: Sima Yi, staying behind at Xuchang, is to 「督後諸軍，錄後臺文書事」, while Chen Qun accompanies the imperial carriage and is to 「董督衆軍，錄行尚書事」[34] — i.e. to oversee the documents and business of the (rear / travelling) Secretariat. Chen Qun is likewise recorded as holding the charge: 「以羣爲镇軍大將軍，领中护軍，录尚書事」[30].

For Zhuge Liang himself: 「亮以丞相錄尚書事，假節」[2] — he was Chancellor and concurrently oversaw Secretariat affairs. After Liu Bei's death, 「及備殂沒，嗣子幼弱，事無巨細，亮皆專之」[27]; and from 建興元年 (the year the text assigns to this), 「封亮武鄉侯，開府治事。頃之，又領益州牧。政事無巨細，咸決於亮」[25].

So, on the evidence: the charge chiefly meant taking part in and supervising the Secretariat's handling of state documents and the routine conduct of government business — the issuing and receiving of commands and the review of papers passing through that office. That is what the title itself denoted. That in Zhuge Liang's case it in practice came to mean deciding all civil affairs, great and small, is an inference: it follows from the fact that he held it together with the chancellorship and the governorship of Yi province while the heir was young [2][25][27], not from the wording of the title *lu shangshu shi* alone.

q: Which present-day city roughly corresponds to Jianye of the Three Kingdoms period? What is the city that served as Shu-Han's capital called today?
reply:
**Jianye (建業)** corresponds to today's **Nanjing (南京市, Jiangsu Province)**; **Shu-Han's capital Chengdu (成都)** is still called **Chengdu (成都市, Sichuan Province)** — the name has not changed.

On the textual basis for the two capitals:

Jianye was originally called Moling (秣陵). The Wu record states that in Jian'an 16 Sun Quan moved his seat there, and the next year built a fortress and renamed it: 「十六年，權徙治秣陵。明年，城石頭，改秣陵爲建業」[5]. He had earlier returned from the campaign against Guan Yu and made Wuchang his capital — 「權破羽還，都武昌」[1] — and later moved the capital to Jianye, as the text records: 「秋九月，權遷都建業，因固府不改館」[4]; the Zhu Ju biography likewise says 「黃龍元年，權遷都建業」[10]. Sun Shao's biography notes that after the Wuchang period, when Sun Quan "returned to Jianye," Sun Shao was at last able to have an audience with him: 「權還建業，乃得朝覲」[3].

Chengdu was Liu Bei's base after he took Yi Province — the Shu record says Liu Zhang surrendered and 「先主复領益州牧」, and that when Liu Bei went out, Zhuge Liang 「常鎮守成都，足食足兵」[12][17]. Liu Bei took the imperial title there: 「即皇帝位於成都武擔之南」[11], and after his death Liu Shan succeeded him in Chengdu: 「五月，後主襲位於成都，時年十七」[15].

One caveat: the *Sanguozhi* text itself gives only the ancient names — that Jianye corresponds to modern Nanjing, and Chengdu to modern Chengdu, is a matter of present-day geography rather than something stated in the text.

q: In the title 'Marquis of Hanshou Village' (Hanshou tinghou), is 'Marquis' an office or a rank of nobility? Did Guan Yu's receiving this title mean that he served as Prefect of Hanshou county?
reply:
侯 (marquis) in "Hanshou tinghou" is a rank of nobility (爵), not an office (官); and no — receiving it did not make Guan Yu the Prefect of Hanshou. His actual office at that moment was a military one, 偏將軍.

What the text records: 「曹公禽羽以歸，拜為偏將軍，禮之甚厚」…「曹公即表封羽為漢壽亭侯」[1] — Cao Gong captured Yu and brought him back, appointed (拜) him Lieutenant-General, and then memorialized (表) to enfeoff (封) him as Marquis of Hanshou Village. The two different verbs matter: 拜 is used for the office, 封 for the noble title. The 表 also matters — the title was formally conferred by the Han court on Cao Cao's recommendation.

The sources consistently keep office and nobility in separate slots. In a memorial list of officials we read 「前將軍都亭侯臣袁綝」[21] — 前將軍 is the post, 都亭侯 the noble title. In the 武帝紀: 「始置名號侯至五大夫，與舊列侯、關內侯凡六等，以賞軍功」[15] — the grades from 名號侯 down to 五大夫, together with the old 列侯 and 關內侯, six grades in all, used to reward military merit; 裴注引《魏書》 on this describes their seals and ribbons [32]. Earlier, 「大封功臣二十餘人，皆爲列侯」[37].

That 亭侯 is a grade of noble title is also clear from the 后妃傳 preface, which gives palace ladies' noble equivalents: 「昭華比鄉侯；脩容比亭侯」[17]. And 裴松之, doubting a Han-time story, says 「漢高祖時封皆列侯，未有鄉亭之爵」[33] — at Gaozu's time enfeoffments were all 列侯, there were no 鄉/亭 noble titles yet. So 鄉侯、亭侯 are subdivisions of 列侯, i.e. grades of nobility.

Marquises of this kind held revenue households (食邑), not administrative authority: 「紹封攸孫彪爲陵樹亭侯，邑三百戸」[19]; 「詔封恕子預爲豐樂亭侯，邑百户」[41]. From this one can infer that a 亭侯 drew the taxes of a set number of households in the place named in his title. In the records I found, no 亭侯 is shown governing his fief, while offices like 太守 are always recorded separately — as when Liu Bei later made Guan Yu 「襄陽太守、蕩寇將軍」[16]. It is an inference, not something the text states, that if Cao Cao had meant him to run Hanshou the record would have said 拜羽為漢壽令/長.

So: "Hanshou tinghou" is a noble title of the 亭侯 grade, named after the place Hanshou; the 侯 here is a peerage, and Guan Yu was not thereby Prefect of Hanshou.

q: Which cities normally served as the capitals of Ts'ao-Wei, Shu-Han and Sun-Wu respectively? For Wu, give the capital used over the long term after Sun Ch'üan moved the court.
reply:
**Short answer.** Cao-Wei's capital was Luoyang; Shu-Han's was Chengdu; and Sun-Wu's long-term capital after Sun Quan's move was Jianye (modern Nanjing). Before Jianye, Sun Quan ruled from Gong'an and then from Wuchang.

**Cao-Wei — Luoyang.** In the twelfth month of the first year of Huangchu, right after Cao Pi ascended the imperial throne, he began building the Luoyang palace and went there: 「十二月，初營洛陽宮，戊午幸洛陽」[3] — "In the twelfth month he first built the Luoyang palace; on the day *wuwu* he arrived at Luoyang." Earlier, Cao Cao had kept the Han emperor at Xu, 「董昭等勸太祖都許」[1], and the pre-dynastic Wei fief was seated at Ye, where Cao Cao resided, 「二十一年春二月，公還鄴」[2], and where 「夏五月，天子進公爵爲魏王」[2]. As a dynasty, however, Wei's seat was Luoyang.

**Shu-Han — Chengdu.** Liu Bei took the throne there: 「即皇帝位於成都武擔之南」[22] — "He ascended the imperial throne south of Wudan in Chengdu." After his death his heir did the same: 「五月，後主襲位於成都」[26] — "In the fifth month the Later Ruler succeeded to the throne in Chengdu."

**Sun-Wu — Jianye.** Sun Quan first shifted from Gong'an to E, renaming it Wuchang: 「權自公安都鄂，改名武昌」[14] — "Sun Quan moved his capital from Gong'an to E, renaming it Wuchang." He then walled that city (「八月，城武昌」[14]). In the fourth month of the first year of Huanglong he ascended the imperial throne, 「丙申，南郊即皇帝位」[15]. That autumn he moved downriver: 「秋九月，權遷都建業，因固府不改館，徵上大將軍陸遜輔太子登，掌武昌留事」[11] — "In the ninth month of autumn Sun Quan moved the capital to Jianye, using the existing offices without rebuilding the residences, and summoned the Grand General Lu Xun to assist the Heir Sun Deng and take charge of the Wuchang rear." This is the move the question asks about. That Jianye remained the seat is shown by the block that follows the move being dated 「二年春正月」[11] — 由此看, that is the second year of Huanglong, with Jianye still the court — and by later notices: Hu Zong 「權下都建業，詳、綜並為侍中」[13], and Sun Shao, who had not had an audience for over a decade, 「權還建業，乃得朝覲」[17]. Sun Quan's own decree calls Jianye his palace city: 「建業宮乃朕從京來所作將軍府寺耳」[20] (裴注引《江表傳》).

One qualification, all from what I found: Wuchang remained a secondary base and was rebuilt later. 裴松之按 notes 「孫權赤烏十年，詔徙武昌宮材瓦，以繕治建康宮」, and 裴注引《吳錄》 says 「諸葛恪有遷都意，更起武昌宮」[19] — so there were later building works and at least a stated intention of moving back, but the capital after Sun Quan's move is given in the record as Jianye.

q: Can the 'Jing Province' of the late Eastern Han be equated directly with today's Jingzhou city in Hubei? Explain how the two differ as geographical concepts.
reply:
No — they are two different kinds of thing. The late-Han "Jing Province" (荊州) was a province-level division (one of the 州), a huge territory spanning several modern provinces; today's Jingzhou City in Hubei is a single prefecture-level city on the middle Yangtze. That last point is modern geography, not something the sources state; from the records below it can be inferred that the modern city sits only within the old Nan Commandery/Jiangling core of the province.

**荊州 was the unit of office — a province run by an Inspector (刺史) or Shepherd (牧), not a city.** Liu Biao's biography: 「靈帝崩，代王叡爲荊州刺史」[12]; later Li Jue and Guo Si made him 「鎮南將軍、荊州牧」[11]. Below the province sat commanderies with their own 太守 — e.g. 「長沙太守張羨叛表」[11], and 糜芳「爲南郡太守」[25].

**Its subordinate units were commanderies spread over what are now several provinces.** The text names 長沙、零陵、桂陽、南郡、江夏、武陵: 「分荊州、江夏、長沙、桂陽東屬，南郡、零陵、武陵西屬」[18]; 諸葛亮 was set to oversee 「零陵、桂陽、長沙三郡」[22]. The province's extent under Liu Biao: 「南收零、桂，北據漢川，地方數千里，帶甲十餘萬」[11].

**Liu Biao based himself at Xiangyang, not at today's Jingzhou.** 「是時山東兵起，表亦合兵軍襄陽」[12]. Xiangyang is a different modern city, further north in Hubei. Jiangling, inside today's Jingzhou City area, appears as a commandery-level centre within the province: Cao Cao 「公進軍江陵，下令荊州吏民，與之更始」[14]; 士仁 was stationed at 公安 nearby [25].

**After 208 "荊州" became a contested political label, not one fixed place.** It was carved up: 「分荊州、江夏、長沙、桂陽東屬，南郡、零陵、武陵西屬」[18], while Cao Cao's side 「留曹仁、徐晃於江陵，使樂進守襄陽」[31]. So "Jing Province" in the Three Kingdoms period meant a shifting set of commanderies held by Cao, Liu and Sun at once — nothing like a single municipality.

In short: in the late Eastern Han, 荊州 was a province (州) of many commanderies across central-south China, its holder based at Xiangyang; the modern city of Jingzhou corresponds at most to the old Jiangling/Nan Commandery core inside it, and equating the two would be like equating a whole province with one of its cities.

q: Is Hanzhong north or south of the Qinling mountains? Why was it such an important region for Shu-Han, both for defending against attack from the north and for sending armies northward?
reply:
**Yes — Hanzhong lies south of the Qinling range**, on the Han (Mian) river, with the Qinling wall to its north. The texts make the direction of travel plain. Wei Yan's plan against Chang'an had to go around the range:「直從褒中出，循秦嶺而東，當子午而北」[3] — out from Baozhong, east along the Qinling, and only then north through the Ziwu pass. Cao Cao came at Hanzhong from the other side:「王自長安出斜谷，軍遮要以臨漢中，遂至陽平」[5] — out of Chang'an through Xie Valley to Yangping. And Liu Bei, fighting for the region, moved from Yangping southward across the Mian:「二十四年春，自陽平南渡沔水，緣山稍前，於定軍山勢作營」[43]. Northward to the Guanzhong plain you cross the Qinling by passes such as Xie, Ziwu or Luogu (Zhong Hui's army came in by 斜谷、駱谷, with a detachment sent 趣子午谷 [47]); southward into the Sichuan basin you go by Yangping pass and, farther west, by the Yinping bypath, with Jiange beyond [48][55]. Hanzhong's own seat was Nanzheng: when Cao Cao took the region,「公軍入南鄭，盡得魯府庫珍寶」[39].

**As a shield for Shu.** Yang Hong stated the stakes when Liu Bei was urgently calling for troops:「漢中則益州咽喉，存亡之機會，若無漢中則無蜀矣，此家門之禍也」[13] — Hanzhong is Yizhou's throat; without it there is no Shu. Liu Ye argued the same point from Cao Cao's side: take Hanzhong and「蜀人望風，破膽失守，推此而前，蜀可傳檄而定」; hesitate, and Shu would「據險守要」and become unassailable [1]. It was the outer gate of the basin.

**As a base for striking north.** Fa Zheng's argument for seizing it gives the classic rationale:「上可以傾覆寇敵，尊獎王室，中可以蠶食雍、涼，廣拓境土，下可以固守要害，為持久之計」[19]. That is how it was used. Zhuge Liang moved his army there in 建興五年:「五年，率諸軍北駐漢中」[12], and from there fought the Qishan campaigns, the siege of Chencang by way of San Pass, and finally the Xie Valley advance to Wuzhang Plain:「六年春，亮出攻祁山，不克。冬，復出散關，圍陳倉，糧盡退」[9]「十二年春，亮悉大眾由斜谷出，以流馬運，據武功五丈原」[27]. It was also his logistics base: in 建興十一年「亮使諸軍運米，集於斜谷口，治斜谷邸閣」[30]. Jiang Wei followed the same pattern, stationed in Hanzhong under Jiang Wan and repeatedly leading troops out into Longxi, Nan'an and Jincheng:「又出隴西、南安、金城界」[56].

**The defensive system and Jiang Wei's revision.** Liu Bei left Wei Yan at Hanzhong with troops distributed among the forward posts:「先主留魏延鎮漢中，皆實兵諸圍以御外敵。敵若來攻，使不得入」[8]. Wang Ping beat off Cao Shuang's ten-plus armies at Xingshi under this system, with「時漢中守兵不滿三萬」[7]. Jiang Wei changed it: on the enemy's approach the posts were to gather troops and grain and withdraw to the two cities of Han and Le —「諸圍皆斂兵聚谷，退就漢、樂二城」— letting the enemy into the plain and striking his weakness, which he called「此殄敵之術也」[8]. In the invasion of 景元四年 the Shu posts indeed did not fight but「退還漢、樂二城守」, and Zhong Hui「會徑過，西出陽安口」[47]; after「蔣舒開城出降，傅僉格鬥而死」the passes were lost, Jiang Wei could only hold Jiange, and Zhong Hui was in fact considering withdrawal —「會不能克，糧運縣遠，將議還歸」— before Deng Ai came in by the Yinping bypath [46][55][48].

**Whether the revision itself doomed Shu the sources debate but do not settle.** Sun Sheng held that Jiang Wei「居禦侮之任而致敵喪守」, and on the score of wisdom and courage「於夫智勇，莫可云也」[65]. Liao Hua had warned「兵不戢，必自焚」[66], and Fei Yi had told Jiang Wei not to stake everything on one throw:「若不如志，悔之無及」[71]. Pei Songzhi's note to the Jiang Wei biography records that Zhuge Zhan and Dong Jue wanted him recalled and stripped of command:「瞻、厥等以維好戰無功，國內疲弊，宜表後主，召還為益州刺史，奪其兵權」[59]. Pei Songzhi himself rebuts Sun Sheng: with Zhong Hui stopped at Jiange and already discussing retreat,「全蜀之功，幾乎立矣」, and the real cause was Deng Ai's flank march, so「而責維不能奮節綿竹，擁衛蜀主，非其理也」[52]. What the sources state as fact is that the passes fell and Deng Ai's Yinping march decided the campaign; that the change of system was itself the cause is an inference, not something the texts say — the recorded verdicts conflict, and the outcome turned on the fall of Yang'an pass and the road through Yinping.

q: Jiange chiefly controls traffic between which two regions? Why is it so well suited to defense?
reply:
Jiange (劍閣) sits on the road that links Hanzhong and the north — the Guanzhong side, whose armies entered through the Xie and Luo valleys ("分從斜谷、駱谷入" [35]) — with the Shu heartland in the Chengdu plain. In the sources it is where the Shu army, falling back from Hanzhong and Yinping, made its stand: "皆退保劍閣以拒會" [6], and "與蜀將張翼、廖化等合守劍閣拒會" [19].

Why it was so hard to force:

**It lay on the direct road into the plain.** Deng Ai's memorial shows Jiange could not simply be turned: he proposed to go around by a side path, "從陰平由邪徑經漢德陽亭趣涪，出劍閣西百里，去成都三百餘里", using a "奇兵" that came out 100 li west of Jiange and still 300-odd li from Chengdu [1]. The bypass itself is called a "邪徑", and Deng Ai is said to have entered "自陰平由景谷道傍入" [13] and to have come in "詭道傍入" [4] — from which one may infer that the ordinary, direct route ran through Jiange.

**Terrain let a smaller force hold a much larger one.** The defenders "列營守險" and "保險拒守" — camping in line and holding the natural defiles [13][3]. The result is recorded plainly: with 鍾會's host at Jiange, "會不得進，已議還計" [4], and "鍾會以二十萬眾留劍閣而不得進，三軍之士已飢" [25]. The place could not be taken by assault, and 鍾會 "糧運縣遠，將議還歸" — his supply line was stretched so far that he was about to discuss withdrawing [13]. Deng Ai's own plan assumed that so long as Jiange held, the only alternatives were that the garrison would be drawn back to relieve Fu, letting 鍾會 "方軌而進", or that it would stay, leaving Fu weakly held [1].

So the defensive value is documented in two ways: the road through Jiange was the direct route into Shu, and a large army could neither storm the defile nor feed itself in front of it. What finally broke Shu was not the taking of Jiange but Deng Ai's bypass through the Yinping side road to Mianzhu — a route the sources themselves present as the exceptional way around, which is the measure of how well Jiange served as the gate. (That a narrow gorge also kept a big army from deploying its numbers is a reasonable inference from "據險/守險" together with the recorded failure of a force given as 200,000 strong, but it is inference, not a statement in the text.)

q: Why was Sima Yi able to be enshrined in the Ancestral Temple of Cao Cao (to share in the sacrifices to the Wei founder)?
reply:
**Short answer:** According to the *Sanguozhi*, Sima Yi was not singled out by name in some special act of grace. The officials proposed that the meritorious ministers who were to share in the sacrifices in the temple of Taizu (Cao Cao) be re-ordered *by office*, and because Sima Yi was Grand Tutor (太傅) and "功高爵尊," his merit high and his rank honoured, he was placed at the very top. This came in the same year as his death.

**The record.** In the *Wei shu*, Annals of the Qi Prince (三少帝紀), under Jiaping 3 (251 CE, per the era conversion):

「十一月，有司奏諸功臣應饗食於太祖廟者，更以官為次，太傅司馬宣王功高爵尊，最在上。」[3]

(*In the 11th month the officials memorialized that the meritorious ministers who should share in the sacrifices in the temple of Taizu be re-arranged by office; the Grand Tutor, Sima Xuan-wang, whose merit was high and rank honoured, was placed at the top.*) The same passage records that Sima Yi had died in the 7th month of that year, and that Sima Shi was then made 撫軍大將軍、錄尚書事 [3].

**The underlying rule.** Enshrinement in Taizu's temple court was an established Wei practice, not something devised for Sima Yi. Under Qinglong 1, Mingdi decreed that the late General-in-Chief Xiahou Dun, Grand Marshal Cao Ren and General of Chariots and Cavalry Cheng Yu be sacrificed in Taizu's temple court [25], and Pei Songzhi's note quotes the *Wei shu* decree stating the criterion:

「大魏元功之臣功勳優著，終始休明者，其皆依禮祀之。」[8]

(*The great founding ministers of Wei whose merit was outstanding and whose conduct was fair and bright from first to last shall all be sacrificed to according to ritual.*) Sima Yi's placement follows this decree, and the ground the text gives is merit together with the dignity of his office.

**What his contemporaries said his merits were.** In a memorial that Cao Shuang had his brother Cao Xi submit, three grounds were given for treating Sima Yi as senior to Cao Shuang himself: his "名足鎮衆，義足率下"; his "包懷大略，允文允武，仍立征伐之勳"; and his "萬里旋斾，親受遺詔，翼亮皇家" — returning from afar to receive the deathbed charge and support the imperial house [26]. Later, even the rebels Guanqiu Jian and Wen Qin, while indicting Sima Shi, conceded of the father: 「故相國懿，匡輔魏室，歷事忠貞，故烈祖明皇帝授以寄託之任」[4].

**Two things to keep separate.** The text records the grounds as merit and rank, and the proposal as coming from the officials (有司奏); it does not say who decided, nor why at that moment. From the fact that in the same year's entries Sima Shi was given 撫軍大將軍、錄尚書事 right after his father's death [3], one can infer that the Sima family already stood at the head of the court — but the text does not state that this caused the placement, and I would not treat the coincidence as proof of cause. Note also that Pei Songzhi himself had reservations about these lists in general, saying he could not understand why some men were promoted and others passed over [1]; his remark concerns Xun Yu, Cheng Yu, Guo Jia and others, not Sima Yi, but it shows the placements were contested rather than self-evident.
