q: How does the Records of the Three Kingdoms tell the story of the "belt edict" (the secret edict hidden in Emperor Xian's belt), and why did Liu Bei not mention it when he proclaimed himself emperor?
reply:
Short answer: the premise needs a correction. The *Records* does tell the belt-edict story in full, and Liu Bei's side did invoke it publicly — but in the 建安二十四年 documents around his taking the title King of Hanzhong, not in the 建安二十六年 proclamation of the imperial title, which rests on a different argument.

**The story as the *Records* tells it.** In Liu Bei's biography: 「先主未出時，獻帝舅車騎將軍董承辭受帝衣帶中密詔，當誅曹公」[1]. Liu Bei then joined the plot with Dong Cheng, Zhong Ji, Wu Zilan and Wang Zifu, but was sent out before it could be launched: 「會見使，未發。事覺，承等皆伏誅」[1]. Pei Songzhi notes that Dong Cheng was a nephew of Empress Dowager Dong and thus Xian's father-in-law, "舅" being the old usage [3]. Pei's note citing the 《華陽國志》 preserves Liu Bei's cover line about the thunderclap: 「聖人云『迅雷風烈必變』，良有以也。一震之威，乃可至於此也！」[31], and the note citing the 《獻帝起居注》 preserves Dong Cheng's recruiting talk with Wang Zifu [8]. Cao Cao's own biography confirms it from the other side — 「備之未東也，陰與董承等謀反」[11] — and dates the collapse: 「五年春正月，董承等謀泄，皆伏誅」[12].

**Where Liu Bei's side did mention it.** When the officials urged him to take the title King of Hanzhong (建安二十四年, cf. 「建安二十四年，先主為漢中王」[19]), their memorial to Emperor Xian says of him: 「睹其機兆，赫然憤發，與車騎將軍董承同謀誅操，將安國家，克寧舊都」[7]. Liu Bei's own answering memorial says the same: 「臣昔與車騎將軍董承圖謀討操，機事不密，承見陷害，臣播越失據，忠義不果」[6]. So the belt edict was very much part of his public case at that point.

**In the enthronement documents it does not appear.** The text he swore at Chengdu says: 「今曹操阻兵安忍，戮殺主後，滔天泯夏，罔顧天顯」, and then 「操子丕，載其凶逆，竊居神器」[24]. The memorial of Xu Jing, Zhuge Liang and the rest urging him on opens with 「曹丕篡弒，湮滅漢室，竊據神器」[18]. The grounds offered are Cao Pi's usurpation, the portents, and the need for a Han heir — not the old plot against Cao Cao. I found no mention of Dong Cheng in these enthronement texts.

**Why the shift — this part is inference, since the *Records* states no reason.** Three recorded facts bear on it. First, the plot had collapsed in 建安五年正月 [12]; by the 建安二十六年 enthronement that was over twenty years past, and Dong Cheng and the other conspirators were long dead. Second, the immediate occasion had changed: 「或傳聞漢帝見害，先主乃發喪制服，追諡曰孝愍皇帝」[27] — a rumour that Emperor Xian had been killed, which Liu Bei mourned in 建安二十五年. Third, Pei's note citing the 《典略》 records that Liu Bei sent Han Ran to condole on Cao Cao's death and 「備得報書，遂稱制」[17], which fits a man positioning himself as the legitimate Han successor rather than as executor of an old conspiracy. Putting these together, the change looks like a shift of rhetorical ground rather than a denial: in 建安二十四年 the belt edict served to show his loyalty to Emperor Xian; by 建安二十六年 the stronger claim was that Cao Pi had stolen the dynasty and a man of the Liu house had to carry it on. Note also that in the *Records* Emperor Xian was in fact not killed — he was enfeoffed as Duke of Shanyang, 「以河內之山陽邑萬戶奉漢帝爲山陽公」[34], and lived on until 青龍年間 [32]; the rumour Liu Bei acted on was just that, a rumour.

In short: the *Records* records the belt edict in full, and Liu Bei's side did cite it — but in the 建安二十四年 memorials, not at the 建安二十六年 enthronement, where the justification had moved to Cao Pi's usurpation and the continuity of the Han.

q: What rank of strategist was Guo Jia, really, under Cao Cao?
reply:
**Short answer:** In formal rank, Guo Jia was never one of the great "military instructor" (軍師) officers. The only office his biography records is **司空軍祭酒** — Army Libationer in the office of the Minister of Works (Cao Cao's own 司空府), a staff-adviser post; later documents simply call him 軍祭酒. He also held the noble title 洧陽亭侯. So "strategist" describes his function and influence rather than a high formal rank — though in terms of Cao Cao's personal trust he stood at the very top.

**What the record actually gives him**

Xun Yu recommended him; after Cao Cao interviewed him he said 「使孤成大業者，必此人也」[8] ("the one who will make my great enterprise succeed must be this man"), and then 「表為司空軍祭酒」[8] — Cao Cao memorialized the throne and appointed him Army Libationer of the Minister of Works. That is the only appointment his biography records during his life. The title itself shows he was an officer within Cao Cao's 司空 office (that much is inference from the wording of the title, not a statement in the text).

His noble rank came after the campaigns against Yuan Tan and Yuan Shang: 「封嘉洧陽亭侯」[6]. When he died — 「年三十八，自柳城還，疾篤」, i.e. at thirty-eight, after returning from Liucheng — Cao Cao's memorial speaks of 「軍祭酒郭嘉，自從征伐，十有一年」 and asks that his fief be raised by 800 households, 「並前千戶」, to 1,000 in all; his posthumous title was 貞侯 [1].

**Why he still counts as top-tier**

Cao Cao's own words treat him as a confidant he meant to leave his affairs to: 「天下事竟，欲以後事屬之」[1] ("when the affairs of the world were settled, I meant to entrust my after-affairs to him"). Writing to Xun Yu, Cao Cao said 「郭奉孝年不滿四十，相與周旋十一年」 and again 「欲以後事屬之，何意卒爾失之」[17], adding that his grasp of current affairs and military matters 「過絕於人」 — far surpassed others. After the return from Jingzhou, at Baqiu, Cao Cao sighed 「郭奉孝在，不使孤至此」[4].

Later, the record of the last Wei emperor contains an edict: 「是歲，詔祀故軍祭酒郭嘉於太祖廟庭」[5] — sacrifices to the late Army Libationer Guo Jia were ordered performed in the temple courtyard of Taizu. From this it can be inferred that being sacrificed in Cao Cao's own temple court was an exceptional posthumous honour; note that the edict itself still styles him 軍祭酒, the modest office.

**How Chen Shou ranked him**

Chen Shou's verdict groups him with the talented planners rather than the great administrators: 「程昱、郭嘉、董昭、劉曄、蔣濟才策謀略，世之奇士，雖清治德業，殊於荀攸，而籌畫所料，是其倫也」[37] — in talent and strategic planning they were "remarkable men of the age"; though in purity of governance and moral achievement they differed from Xun You, in planning and foresight they were of the same class.

**The distinction to draw**

Formally, his post was a relatively modest one within the 司空府: he never became 軍師 or 中軍師 as Xun You did — Xun You's biography records 「以為軍師」 and later 「轉爲中軍師」[19]. Functionally, Cao Cao treated him as his closest planner and intended to entrust him with his affairs after his death, and he was eventually enshrined in Cao Cao's temple.

One caveat worth noting from the record: Chen Qun repeatedly attacked him at court for 「不治行檢」 (not cultivating his conduct), and Cao Cao 「愈益重之」, valued him all the more, while also approving of Chen Qun's uprightness [4]. Chen Shou's remark that his 清治德業 differed from Xun You probably points at exactly this. A second caveat: some of the credit later sources give him is disputed — 裴松之按, comparing 《傅子》 with the 《武帝紀》, says the decision to march east against Liu Bei and the judgement that Yuan Shao would not come out 「皆出自太祖」, so that 《傅子》's attribution of the plan to Guo Jia 「則為不同」[35]. So his reputation as Cao Cao's indispensable strategist rests on Cao Cao's own testimony and on the honours paid him, not on a high rank or on every campaign decision being his.

q: If Cao Shuang had followed Huan Fan's advice, could the Incident at the Gaoping Tombs have been avoided?
reply:
**Short answer:** The sources never record what would have happened had Cao Shuang followed Huan Fan's plan, so the question can only be answered by inference. Two things can be said from the record. First, the coup had already been launched before Cao Shuang had to choose — Huan Fan's advice could only have decided how the affair ended, not prevented it. Second, the text presents Cao Shuang's surrender, not the soundness of Huan Fan's plan, as the immediate occasion of his destruction; whether resistance would have saved him is left open.

**What the record says.** In the first month of the first year of Jiaping the imperial carriage went to pay homage at the Gaoping Tombs, and Sima Yi memorialized to strip Cao Shuang and his brothers of office: 「嘉平元年春正月甲午，車駕謁高平陵。太傅司馬宣王奏免大將軍曹爽……」[6]. Sima Yi first seized the arsenal and then camped at the Luo River floating bridge: 「宣王部勒兵馬，先據武庫，遂出屯洛水浮橋」[30]; in his own memorial he says 「臣輙力疾，將兵屯洛水浮橋，伺察非常」[45]. Gao Rou was given the empress dowager's edict to act as general and occupy Cao Shuang's camp: 「皇太后詔召柔假節行大將軍事，據爽營」[14], and Wang Guan was made acting commander of the central army to occupy Cao Xi's camp: 「司馬宣王誅爽，使觀行中領軍，據爽弟羲營」[43].

Huan Fan got out through the Pingchang gate, which was already shut — 「突出至平昌城門，城門已閉」[9] — and urged Cao Shuang to take the emperor to Xu Chang and summon outside troops: 「範說爽使車駕幸許昌，招外兵」[1]. He pressed Cao Xi: 「當今日，卿門戶求貧賤復可得乎？且匹夫持質一人，尚欲望活，今卿與天子相隨，令於天下，誰敢不應者？」[1] He added concrete assets — Cao Xi's separate camp south of the palace gate, the Luoyang farming office outside the city, the Xu Chang arsenal, and, for the grain problem, 「大司農印章在我身」[9]. The answer was silence: 「羲兄弟默然不從，中夜至五鼓，爽乃投刀於地」[9]. Cao Shuang said he guessed the Grand Tutor merely wanted them to submit — 「我度太傅意，亦不過欲令我兄弟向己也」— and told the emperor to issue the edict removing his office [9]. His registrar Yang Zong also tried to stop him: 「公挾主握權，捨此以至東巿乎？」[8]

Sima Yi's side had already made its judgment: 「範畫策，爽必不能用範計」[1]; to Jiang Ji he said 「智囊往矣」, and Jiang Ji replied 「範則智矣，駑馬戀棧豆，爽必不能用也」[4]. Xu Yun and Chen Tai then urged Cao Shuang to surrender, Jiang Ji wrote conveying Sima Yi's meaning, and Yin Damu was sent to tell Cao Shuang it was 「唯免官而已，以洛水爲誓」; Cao Shuang believed it and disbanded his troops [4]. Afterwards he said 「我不失作富家翁」[4], and only then came the Zhang Dang confession, the charge of plotting rebellion, and the execution of Cao Shuang with three clans wiped out [6][7].

**What can be inferred.** Since the memorial to depose Cao Shuang, the seizure of the arsenal, the occupation of both brothers' camps and the camp at the Luo River bridge all precede Huan Fan's arrival, Huan Fan's plan could not have prevented the Incident; it could only have changed its outcome. That much follows from the sequence above. What the plan's success would have been is a different question, and here the record gives only partisan claims, not a verdict: Huan Fan's 「誰敢不應者」[1] is a partisan argument, and Sima Yi's memorial likewise claims the great ministers were with him — 「太尉臣濟、尚書令臣孚等，皆以爽為有無君之心」[30]. That the recorded predictions are all about Cao Shuang's character rather than the plan's feasibility, and that Sima Yi thought it worth saying Cao Shuang 「必不能用範計」[1][4], suggests his side did not treat the plan as harmless — but that is inference from what they said, not a statement of the plan's outcome. One further point: in this period the empress dowager's name carried real authority — 「與奪大事，皆先諮啟於太后而後施行」[23] — and Sima Yi acted in her name, which a move to Xu Chang with the emperor would have had to answer with the emperor's person. That too is inference.

So: the sources support saying the text presents Cao Shuang's submission, not the weakness of Huan Fan's advice, as the immediate cause of his destruction. Whether taking the plan would have saved him is something the record leaves open, and the text's only forecasts concern Cao Shuang himself, not the plan.

q: Should Xiahou Ba have defected to Shu Han?
reply:
**Short answer:** The records never pass that judgment themselves — Chen Shou's appraisal of the chapter weighs the Xiahou and Cao houses and faults Cao Shuang and Xiahou Xuan, not Ba's flight [34]. On the evidence, though, his flight is understandable: he was a man marked by his ties to Cao Shuang, with a personal enemy about to become his commanding officer. Whether it was *right* depends on whether you weigh survival above loyalty to Wei; the texts give material for both readings.

**Why he went**

The main text is terse: 「素爲曹爽所厚。聞爽誅，自疑，亡入蜀」[2]. The two facts it stresses are the Cao Shuang connection and his own fear — not any change of allegiance. The Pei note from the *Weilüe* gives the fuller reasoning: he feared the purge would reach him, 「以爲祸必轉相及，心既内恐」, and separately he had long been on bad terms with the Inspector of Yongzhou, Guo Huai, who was now replacing Xiahou Xuan as General Who Conquers the West, so that 「霸尤不安，故遂奔蜀」[09-0008n0]. The same note shows how desperate the escape was: he lost his way heading for Yinping, ran out of food, killed his horse and walked, his feet split open, and he lay under a rock until 「蜀聞之，乃使人迎霸」[09-0008n0]. The Shu record dates it: 「十二年春正月，魏誅大將軍曹爽等，右將軍夏侯霸來降」[10] (Yanxi 12, spring, first month).

**That there was an alternative, and what it carried**

The Pei note citing the *Wei shi chunqiu* preserves the contrast: when Ba was about to flee he called Xiahou Xuan to come with him, and Xuan answered 「吾豈苟存自客於寇虜乎？」 and went back to the capital [27]. Xiahou Xuan was later arrested in the second month of Jiaping 6 over the Li Feng affair and sent to the commandant of justice, with the commandant memorializing that he be punished according to law: 「收玄、緝、鑠、敦、賢等送廷尉」, 「請論如法」[31]. Ba's own son, by contrast, was spared: 「以淵舊勳赦霸子，徙樂浪郡」[2] — though that decision came after the flight and says nothing about what would have happened had he stayed.

**How Shu received him, and what he did there**

Shu received him generously — the *Weilüe* note ends 「厚加爵寵」[4] — partly because of kinship: Ba's younger cousin had been taken by Zhang Fei as wife and bore the daughter who became Liu Shan's empress, so Liu Shan met him with the reassurance 「卿父自遇害於行間耳，非我先人之手刃也」 and pointed out his own son as 「夏侯氏之甥」[09-0008n0]. In Shu he is named as 车骑将军 in the campaign of Yanxi 18, when he and Jiang Wei crushed Wang Jing west of the Tao: 「復與車騎將軍夏侯霸等俱出狄道，大破魏雍州刺史王經於洮西」[23]. Earlier, before the defection, he appears on the Wei side as the officer stationed at Weichi and in the pursuit of Jiang Wei at Tazhong [20][19]. He also gave Shu intelligence on Wei's court, naming Zhong Hui as a danger to Wu and Shu [8]; the Pei note adds that the *Han Jin Chunqiu* version of this is Xizao Chi's elaboration adopted from the *Shishuo*.

**My assessment (inference, not record)**

Weighing these: the move was not a betrayal for gain, and it was not forced by any sentence already passed on him — the texts link him to the Cao Shuang affair only through Cao Shuang's former favor to him. What he had was a well-founded fear of a general purge of Shuang's associates, plus a specific private enemy about to hold command over him. Given that Xiahou Xuan, who stayed and refused to flee, was arrested and had a capital sentence sought against him, it is difficult to argue Ba could have counted on safety by staying. Set against that: by the *Weilüe*'s account he had long been 「霸常切齒，欲有報蜀意」 over his father's death [09-0008n0], so the flight meant reversing a lifelong stance, and he did take up arms against his own state in real battles. From the standpoint of personal survival, the move is defensible; from the standpoint of loyalty to the house his family had served as "flesh and bone" kin — 「夏侯、曹氏，世爲婚姻」, 「並以親舊肺腑，貴重於時」[34] — it is a defection no passage in the text praises. The evidence supports both readings; it settles neither.

q: Li Yan and Zhuge Liang were both regents named in Liu Bei's deathbed charge — so why was Zhuge Liang able to demote Li Yan to a commoner?
reply:
**The short of it:** Li Yan *was* named in the deathbed charge, but as Zhuge Liang's deputy, and his post kept him away from the capital; Zhuge Liang held the substantive machinery of government. When Li Yan's conduct in the campaign of 建興九年 (231) left written evidence and his own admission, Zhuge Liang could and did memorialize for his removal.

The charge itself: in 章武三年 (223) Liu Bei, dying at Yong'an, 「託孤於丞相亮，尚書令李嚴為副」[2]. Li Yan's own biography: 「三年，先主疾病，嚴與諸葛亮並受遺詔輔少主；以嚴為中都護，統內外軍事，留鎮永安」[1]. So both are named, but Li Yan is the deputy, and his office kept him stationed at Yong'an. Liu Bei had also ordered the heir: 「汝與丞相從事，事之如父」[25], and of Zhuge Liang it is recorded that 「及備殂沒，嗣子幼弱，事無巨細，亮皆專之」[6]; he was 丞相、錄尚書事 [24]. 由此看, the asymmetry was institutional rather than a contest between two equals: the man who ran the government and the man posted to the frontier were not in the same position, and the initiative lay with Zhuge Liang.

The immediate cause: in 建興九年 (231) Zhuge Liang's army was at Qishan and Li Yan — who, the biography notes, had changed his name to 李平 [1] — was in charge of transport. Rain broke the supply line: 「秋夏之際，值天霖雨，運糧不繼，平遣參軍狐忠、督軍成籓喻指，呼亮來還；亮承以退軍」. Li Yan then feigned surprise and reported to the throne that the retreat was a ruse: 「平聞軍退，乃更陽驚，說『軍糧饒足，何以便歸』！欲以解己不辦之責，顯亮不進之愆也。又表後主，說『軍偽退，欲以誘賊與戰』」. The decisive point is evidence: 「亮具出其前後手筆書疏本末，平違錯章灼。平辭窮情竭，首謝罪負」[12].

The memorial charged long-standing conduct, not only the grain failure: after Liu Bei's death Li Yan 「所在治家，尚為小惠，安身求名，無憂國之事」; ordered to bring troops to Hanzhong he 「窮難縱橫，無有來意，而求以五郡為巴州刺史」; and asked to oversee Hanzhong he 「說司馬懿等開府闢召」. Zhuge Liang states he had deliberately treated him generously to keep things running: 「正以大事未定，漢室傾危，伐平之短，莫若褒之」. Then 「乃廢平為民，徙梓潼郡」[12]. The removal was executed by a joint document to the 尚書,裴注所引《亮公文上尚書》, carrying over twenty senior officers' names — 劉琰、魏延、吳壹、楊儀、鄧芝、費禕、姜維 and others — 「輒解平任，免官祿、節傳、印綬、符策，削其爵土」[20][18].

Two things follow from the record. First, the punishment was dismissal, not execution, and Zhuge Liang held out restoration: 裴注所引 his letter to Li Yan's son Li Feng says 「若都護思負一意，君與公琰推心從事者，否可複通，逝可複還也」[21]; and when Li Yan heard Zhuge Liang had died he fell ill and died, 「平常冀亮當自補复，策後人不能，故以激憤也」[12]. Second, this was not a private quarrel with one man: 廖立 was likewise 「廢立為民，徙汶山郡」 after a memorial by Zhuge Liang [19], and 裴注引習鑿齒 remarks 「諸葛亮之使廖立垂泣，李平致死，豈徒無怨言而已哉」[22].

So on the records, the "why" is not that Zhuge Liang outranked a co-regent in a showdown, but that the offices were unequal from the start, and the offense of 231 was one Li Yan conceded, with his own letters produced and a broad roster of the Shu leadership endorsing the removal. Chen Shou's verdict on Li Yan is blunt: 「招禍取咎，無不自己也」[15].

q: In the year Ma Su lost Chieh-t'ing, which year of which reign era was Shu-Han using? What year was it on the Wei side? And what year is that in the Western calendar?
reply:
**Short answer:** Shu-Han was using the sixth year of Jianxing (建興六年); Wei was using the second year of Taihe (太和二年); both fall in AD 228.

**Shu-Han's reckoning.** Zhuge Liang's biography in the Shu records the campaign and dates it simply as "the sixth year": 「六年春，揚聲由斜谷道取眉」[4], and then 「亮使馬謖督諸軍在前，與郃戰于街亭」[4], 「謖違亮節度，舉動失宜，大為張郃所破」[4]. Since this passage stands in Zhuge Liang's Shu biography, the "sixth year" is the sixth year of Shu-Han's Jianxing era; this is an inference from the placing of the record, and it is confirmed by Wang Ping's biography, which spells the era out: 「建興六年，屬參軍馬謖先鋒」[2], 「大敗於街亭」[2]. Jianxing 6 = AD 228.

**Wei's reckoning.** Guo Huai's biography in the Wei records the same event by the Wei calendar: 「太和二年，蜀相諸葛亮出祁山，遣將軍馬謖至街亭，高詳屯列柳城。張郃擊謖，淮攻詳營，皆破之」[12]. Zhang He's biography gives the tactical detail: 「謖依阻南山，不下據城。郃絶其汲道，擊，大破之」[17]. Taihe 2 = AD 228.

So it was one and the same year, AD 228, recorded under two different reign eras because Shu and Wei each counted years by their own emperor's era name.

q: Why did the Sun-Liu alliance keep quarreling over Jing Province, until Sun Quan finally stabbed Guan Yu in the back?
reply:
**Short answer:** the Sun–Liu "alliance" was a marriage of convenience against Cao Cao, and Jing Province was the one piece of ground both sides needed for their own security. Wu's own record treats Jing as land Liu Bei borrowed; Liu Bei, made 荊州牧 by his subordinates, treated it as his own [1][8]. Since neither side ever accepted the other's title to it, every round of negotiation ended in a veiled threat or an armed grab, patched up only when Cao Cao forced a truce — that at least is how the records read (this is my inference, not a sentence in the text). By 219 the two things that had restrained Wu — Cao Cao's pressure and Lu Su's policy of keeping Liu Bei as a buffer — had both changed, and Guan Yu's momentum and slights gave Sun Quan his opening.

**The debt was never settled.** Wu's account is that Liu Bei borrowed Jing: 裴注引《江表傳》says 「備以瑜所給地少，不足以安民，復從權借荊州數郡」[1]. Only Lu Su argued for lending it — 「後備詣京見權，求都督荊州，惟肅勸權借之，共拒曹公」[28] — and Sun Quan later called this Lu Su's one fault: 「後雖勸吾借玄德地，是其一短，不足以損其二長也」[34]. Liu Bei, for his part, was 「羣下推先主為荊州牧」[8] after Liu Qi died. Wu therefore always spoke of an unrepaid loan; Liu Bei held it as his own.

**Each round of bargaining was settled by force.** In 建安十九年 (214) Sun Quan, "because Liu Bei had already obtained Yi," had Zhuge Jin demand the Jing commanderies; Liu Bei refused — 「吾方圖涼州，涼州定，乃盡以荊州與吳耳」— and Sun Quan answered 「此假而不反，而欲以虛辭引歳」[2]. Sun Quan 「遂置南三郡長吏」, and 「關羽盡逐之」; Sun Quan sent Lü Meng to take Changsha, Lingling and Guiyang, Liu Bei 「引兵五萬下公安」 and sent Guan Yu 「將三萬兵至益陽」[2][5]. Fighting was averted only because Cao Cao entered Hanzhong: 「會曹公入漢中，備懼失益州，使使求和」[2]. The 建安二十年 (215) line — 「分荊州、江夏、長沙、桂陽東屬，南郡、零陵、武陵西屬」[5] — is recorded as a division made at that moment of alarm, not as a mutually accepted settlement (my inference). The pattern was thus already set four years before the attack on Guan Yu.

**Wu's strategic logic.** Lu Su's position was that Cao Cao was still the real enemy and Liu Bei should be supported as an ally — 裴注引《漢晉春秋》records his argument that 「宜以藉備，使撫安之」, 「多操之敵，而自為樹黨，計之上也」[3]. After Lu Su died, Lü Meng argued the opposite: Guan Yu 「有並兼心，且居國上流，其勢難久」, and it was better to 「取羽，全據長江，形勢益張」 than to take Xuzhou, which Cao's cavalry could contest [21]. Sun Quan 「深納其策」[21]. So for Wu, Jing was not a favor owed back but the high ground above its own territory.

**The immediate trigger, 219.** That year Guan Yu flooded Yu Jin's seven armies, took the prisoners and 「威震華夏」, so that Cao Cao discussed moving the capital; 司馬宣王 and 蔣濟 advised having Sun Quan strike from behind, offering him the south of the river [44]. Sun Quan, who 「內憚羽，外欲以為己功」, wrote offering 「以討羽自效」[22]. Personal friction had already poisoned things: 「先是，權遣使為子索羽女，羽罵辱其使，不許婚，權大怒」[44]; and when Wu's envoys came ostensibly to help at Fan, Guan Yu cursed them — 「鰂子敢爾，如使樊城拔，吾不能滅汝邪！」 — from which Sun Quan 「知其輕己」[47]. Guan Yu had also 「擅取湘關米」[18], and his own subordinates Mi Fang and Shi Ren, who 「素皆嫌羽輕己」, were ready to defect [44][16]. Lü Meng feigned illness [18], Lu Xun's flattering letter left Guan Yu 「意大安，無復所嫌」[25], and the disguised crossing at Xunyang followed [18].

**So why the repeated quarrels, and why the final betrayal?** From these records I would infer two things kept the alliance alive: Cao Cao's threat, and Lu Su's insistence on a buffer. When Cao Cao was weak or distracted, Wu pressed its claim on Jing; when he was strong — Hanzhong in 215, or the Fan campaign of 219, where Wu benefited from Guan Yu bleeding Cao — Wu tolerated the status quo. By late 219 Guan Yu's success had removed his value as a buffer and made him the most dangerous man on Wu's border, which is why Sun Quan chose that moment. That the ownership of Jing was never fixed in terms both sides accepted is, on this reading, the underlying reason each crisis had to be settled by arms; Guan Yu's insults and arrogance are what made the Wu court willing to act. What the text states plainly is only the outcome: 「十二月，璋司馬馬忠獲羽及其子平、都督趙累等於章鄉，遂定荊州」[22], and in Guan Yu's own biography 「權遣將逆擊羽，斬羽及子平於臨沮」[44].

q: Chen Shou was born in Shu, so why does the Records of the Three Kingdoms contain so few accounts of Shu's deeds?
reply:
Chen Shou served Shu — Pei Songzhi's note reports that he had once been a subordinate of Zhuge Zhan [2] — so the question is a fair one, but the premise needs adjusting. The Records does not omit Shu: it contains a Shu section with the annals of the Former Ruler and the Later Ruler. What it lacks is detail, and Chen Shou himself gives the reason — not neglect, but the absence of official record-keeping in Shu.

His appraisal at the end of the Later Ruler's annals says it plainly: 「又國不置史，注記無官，是以行事多遺，災異靡書。」[1] — the state did not establish a history office, and there were no officials charged with keeping records; hence its deeds were largely lost and portents went unrecorded. He adds that even Zhuge Liang, for all his ability in government, did not fully attend to such matters, and that after Zhuge Liang's death 「茲制漸虧，優劣著矣」[1]. This is Chen Shou's own judgment as the compiler, not an outsider's guess.

The gaps struck later readers too. Pei Songzhi, annotating the Former Ruler's biography, laments that the record of Liu Bei's ancestral-temple arrangements is wanting: 「而載記闕略，良可恨哉！」[5]. In a note attached to Xu Ci's biography he quotes Sun Sheng: 「蜀少人士，故慈、潛等並見載述。」[3]

Faced with this, Chen Shou worked from what survived. One source he names is Yang Xi's Ji Han Fu Chen Zan, a set of eulogies written in the Yanxi period: 「戲以延熙四年著《季漢輔臣贊》，其所頌述，今多載於蜀書，是以記之於左。」[14] He notes that men who died after that poem received no further eulogy, so 「或有應見稱紀而不在乎篇者也」, and that for those Yang Xi praised but who have no biography he appended notes under the verse himself [14]. He also compiled and submitted documents to the 著作 office, keeping even 「敵國誹謗之言」 without alteration [11].

Putting this together: the comparative thinness of the Shu section is best explained as a shortage of sources rather than a lack of effort — an inference from Chen Shou's statement about the missing history office [1], Sun Sheng's remark on Shu's few notable men [3], and Pei Songzhi's complaint about missing records [5]. The text does not say outright that Shu's archives were destroyed, and no such claim should be added.

One caution about slant rather than quantity: Pei's note quoting Sun Sheng's Yitong Ji reports the Shu historian Chang Qu saying that Chen Shou had been Zhuge Zhan's subordinate and was humiliated by him, and therefore 「因此事歸惡黃皓，而云瞻不能匡矯也」[2]. That is a third party's assertion about bias, not an established fact, and it concerns how Chen Shou apportioned blame, not how much he wrote.

q: P'ang Te killed Kuo Yüan with his own hand in the battle at P'ing-yang. According to P'ei Sung-chih's commentary, how was Kuo Yüan related to Chung Yao? And how did Chung Yao react when he saw the head — what did he say?
reply:
At the battle of Pingyang, Pang De (龐德, styled Lingming) killed Guo Yuan (郭援) with his own hand: the main text of Pang De's biography says「德為軍鋒，進攻援、幹，大破之，親斬援首」[1], and Ma Chao's biography likewise records「超將龐德親斬援首」[19].

**How they were related.** Pei Songzhi's commentary, quoting the *Weilüe* (《魏略》), says:「援，鍾繇之甥。」[2] — Guo Yuan was Zhong Yao's nephew, i.e. the son of his sister (甥).

**Zhong Yao's reaction to the head.** The same *Weilüe* passage says Pang De cut off a head without knowing whose it was; after the fighting everyone said Guo Yuan was dead but his head could not be found; Pang De then brought a head out of his quiver, and「繇見之而哭」[2] — Zhong Yao wept when he saw it. When Pang De apologized, Zhong Yao answered:

「援雖我甥，乃國賊也。卿何謝之？」[2]

That is: "Although Guo Yuan was my nephew, he was a traitor to the state. Why should you apologize?"

The setting is that Zhong Yao was the Wei commander in this campaign: his biography's main text records his argument against withdrawing and his prediction that the obstinate Guo Yuan would rashly cross the Fen River, followed by「濟水未半，擊，大破之，斬援，降單于」[3]. From this one can infer — it is not stated in the text — that Zhong Yao was directing the operation in which his own nephew was killed, which would fit his treating Guo Yuan in his reply to Pang De as an enemy of the state rather than as kin.

q: How did Cao Pi's Empress Zhen die? Do the historical sources disagree about it?
reply:
Cao Pi's Empress Zhen (文昭甄皇后) was, by Chen Shou's own account, ordered to take her own life — and yes, the sources disagree, both about how she died and about who bore responsibility.

Chen Shou's text is explicit. In the 后妃傳 he writes that after Cao Pi took the throne and favored Guo, Li and Yin, Zhen grew resentful, and that 「踐阼之後，山陽公奉二女以嬪於魏，郭后、李、陰貴人並愛幸，后愈失意，有怨言。帝大怒，二年六月，遣使賜死，葬於鄴。」[18] That second year is Huangchu 2, i.e. 221 AD. In the 郭皇后傳 Chen Shou says plainly that 「甄后之死，由后之寵也」[28], and in the 明帝紀, of her son Cao Rui, that 「以其母誅，故未建為嗣」[33] — Chen Shou himself uses the word 誅, "executed."

Note, though, that the 文帝紀 for the same month records only a bare death notice: 「丁卯，夫人甄氏卒。」[14] — "died," with no mention of an execution.

The dissenting version is preserved by Pei Songzhi from the official Wei history 《魏書》: there Zhen merely fell ill while Cao Pi was putting off her formal installation, and died of sickness. It has the seals and letters sent to her three times and thrice declined — 「璽書三至而后三讓」[20] — and then: 「時盛暑，帝欲須秋涼乃更迎后。會后疾遂篤，夏六月丁卯，崩於鄴。帝哀痛咨嗟，策贈皇后璽綬。」[20] In this version Cao Pi grieves and posthumously grants her the empress's seals; there is no killing at all.

Pei Songzhi himself rejects that version and treats the killing as established: 「文帝之不立甄氏，及加殺害，事有明審」, and he says of the 《魏書》 account that it is 「異乎所聞於舊史」, concluding that its praise of the empresses' virtue cannot be taken at face value [20]. So the disagreement is not merely between two early sources — Pei adjudicates against the Wei court's version.

Harsher details come from works Pei quotes. 《漢晉春秋》 says 「初，甄后之誅，由郭后之寵，及殯，令被髮覆面，以糠塞口，遂立郭后，使養明帝」[24] — at her encoffining she was made to lie with hair covering her face and chaff stuffed in her mouth, and Guo was then made to raise Emperor Ming. It adds that Mingdi, learning of this, repeatedly wept and asked how his mother died; Guo retorted 「先帝自殺，何以責問我？」, whereupon the enraged Mingdi forced her to die and had her buried in the same fashion [24]. 《魏略》 likewise says Mingdi 「追痛甄后之薨」 and ordered Guo's encoffining to follow 「皆如甄后故事」[24]; the 明帝紀 records that the empress dowager died in Qinglong 3 and was buried in the third month [31].

As for the aftermath, when Mingdi took the throne he had an official sacrifice at her tomb and posthumously gave her the title 文昭皇后 — 「癸未，追謚母甄夫人曰文昭皇后」[33], with the 后妃傳 adding that the 司空 was sent 「持節奉策以太牢告祠於陵，又別立寢廟」[27]. In Taihe 4, because her old tomb lay too low, she was reburied at 朝陽陵 [27].

In sum: Chen Shou's narrative, and the 《漢晉春秋》 and 《魏略》 passages Pei quotes, say she was ordered to die, and Pei treats the killing as beyond doubt; the official 《魏書》 says she died of illness. The graphic details about the manner of her death and Guo's responsibility rest on 《漢晉春秋》 and 《魏略》 as quoted by Pei, not on Chen Shou's main text — and Pei, for his part, sided against the Wei court's version.

q: When Liu Pei marched south from Chia-meng against Liu Chang, he left Huo Chün to hold the city. How long did Liu Chang's forces besiege it? How many soldiers did Huo Chün have, and how was the siege finally broken?
reply:
Huo Jun (霍峻) held Jiameng (葭萌) with only a few hundred men; Liu Zhang's generals Fu Jin (扶禁) and Xiang Cun (向存) besieged him for nearly a year without taking the city, and he broke the siege himself, by a sally that killed Xiang Cun.

The account is in Huo Jun's biography: after Liu Bei turned south from Jiameng against Liu Zhang, 「先主自葭萌南還襲劉璋，留峻守葭萌城。」[1] The *Xianzhu zhuan* dates Liu Bei's entry into Yi to 建安十六年 and records that he went north to Jiameng; its next entry opens 「明年，曹公徵孫權，權呼先主自救」[9], and it is in that following year, 建安十七年 = 212 CE, that he turned on Liu Zhang. Before the siege proper, Zhang Lu sent his general Yang Bo to talk Huo Jun into holding the city jointly with him, and Huo Jun answered 「小人頭可得，城不可得。」[1]

On the length of the siege: 「後璋將扶禁、向存等帥萬餘人由閬水上，攻圍攻峻，且一年，不能下」[1] — nearly a year, and the city did not fall.

On Huo Jun's strength: 「峻城中兵才數百人」[1] — only a few hundred men, against the besiegers' 「萬餘人」.

On how it was broken: 「伺其怠隙，選精銳出擊，大破之，即斬存首」[1] — he waited for the besiegers to grow slack and leave an opening, led picked troops out in a sortie, crushed them, and cut off Xiang Cun's head on the spot. 由此看, the city was saved by his own sortie rather than by any relieving force: his biography records no relief army coming to him, only this sally.

Chen Shou's appraisal sums the affair up as 「霍峻孤城不傾」[3]. After Liu Bei pacified Shu he rewarded him, 「分廣漢為梓潼郡，以峻為梓潼太守、裨將軍」[1].

q: Which painter, while painting a screen for Sun Quan, let a drop of ink fall on the silk by mistake and turned it into a fly — so lifelike that Sun Quan took it for a real fly and raised his hand to flick it away?
reply:
The painter was **Cao Buxing (曹不興)**, one of the "Eight Wonders" of Wu.

The story is not in Chen Shou's main text of the *Sanguozhi*; it comes from Pei Songzhi's commentary, which quotes the *Wulu* (《吳錄》), appended to the biography of Zhao Da in the *Wu Shu*:

> 「曹不興善畫，權使畫屏风，誤落筆點素，因就以作蠅。既進御，權以爲生蠅，舉手彈之。」[1]

An English rendering: "Cao Buxing was skilled at painting. Quan [Sun Quan] had him paint a screen; he accidentally let his brush fall and stain the white silk, and so he went along with it and made it into a fly. When it was presented, Quan took it for a live fly and raised his hand to flick it away."

So the account matches your question closely: the blot of ink became a fly so convincing that Sun Quan tried to brush it off. The same passage names the other skilled men of Wu — the calligrapher Huang Xiang, the Go player Yan Wu, the dream-interpreter Song Shou — and says that together with the physiognomist Zheng Yu and Wu Fan, Liu Dun and Zhao Da, eight men in all, they were praised by their contemporaries as the "Eight Wonders" (八絕) [1].

q: Ts'ao Ts'ao asked P'ei Ch'ien about Liu Pei's abilities. How did P'ei Ch'ien assess him?
reply:
**Pei Qian (裴潛) judged Liu Bei as a man who could throw things into disorder but not govern them — dangerous if he ever got an opening and a strong position. When Cao Cao asked him about Liu Bei's ability, he answered: 「使居中國，能亂人而不能爲治也。若乘閒守險，足以爲一方主。」[1] ("Put him in the Central States, and he can disorder men but cannot govern them. If he takes advantage of an opening and holds the strategic terrain, he is enough to be lord of one region.")**

The exchange is in Pei Qian's biography. After Cao Cao pacified Jing Province, he appointed Pei Qian 參丞相軍事; the text then has him serve as magistrate of three counties, enter the office as 倉曹屬, and at that point Cao Cao asked: 「卿前與劉備俱在荊州，卿以備才略何如？」[1] — "You were formerly with Liu Bei in Jing Province; what do you think of Liu Bei's ability and judgment?"

Pei Qian was answering as an eyewitness. The same passage records that he had gone to Jing Province to avoid the troubles, that Liu Biao received him with the courtesy due a guest, and that he privately told those close to him, Wang Can and Sima Zhi: 「劉牧非霸王之才，乃欲西伯自處，其敗無日矣。」[1] From this it can be inferred that Cao Cao was drawing on the observation of a man who had seen Liu Bei at first hand in Jing Province.

This is a different remark from the one Sun Sheng's *Wei shi chunqiu* attributes to Cao Cao himself, that Liu Bei was 「劉備，人傑也，將生憂寡人」[2], where Pei Songzhi notes that recorded speeches are heavily embellished and therefore often untrue: 「史之記言，旣多潤色，故前載所述有非實者矣」[2]. The question here concerns Pei Qian's own answer, which stands in the main text of his biography.

q: When Liu Bei was gravely ill, Huang Yuan, the Grand Administrator of Hanjia, rebelled and burned Linqiong. How did Yang Hong work out where Huang Yuan would go, and how was he captured?
reply:
Yang Hong reasoned from Huang Yuan's character rather than from geography: because Huang Yuan was cruel and had won no one's loyalty, he could neither besiege Chengdu nor seize the south; he would only go downstream eastward, where a single block at the Nan'an gorge would take him.

The main account is Yang Hong's biography [1]. When Liu Bei was already emperor, had failed in his campaign against Wu and was staying at Yong'an, Huang Yuan, Administrator of Hanjia, who was "素為諸葛亮所不善" (long disliked by Zhuge Liang), heard Liu Bei was ill, feared trouble later, and "舉郡反，燒臨邛城" — raised his commandery in revolt and burned Linqiong. Zhuge Liang had gone east to visit the sick, so Chengdu was empty and Huang Yuan was all the bolder. Yang Hong immediately reported to the crown prince, sent the crown prince's own troops, and had the generals Chen Hu and Zheng Chuo attack him.

Others guessed that if Huang Yuan could not besiege Chengdu he would go by way of Yuexi and occupy the south. Yang Hong disagreed [1]:

> 「元素信凶暴，無他恩信，何能辦此？不過乘水東下，冀主上平安，面縛歸死；如其有異，奔吳求活耳。敕曶、綽但於南安峽口遮即便得矣。」

("Huang Yuan is indeed fierce and violent, with no kindness or trustworthiness to his name — how could he accomplish that? He will do no more than ride the water eastward: if he hopes the sovereign recovers he will bind his own hands and come back to die; if things turn out otherwise he will flee to Wu to seek survival. Order Chen Hu and Zheng Chuo simply to block him at the mouth of the Nan'an gorge, and he will be taken.")

So his reasoning rested on two points: Huang Yuan had no popular base, so he could not hold the south; and his only courses were to surrender if Liu Bei lived or flee to Wu if Liu Bei died — both, by my reading of the passage, carrying him downstream, which is why Yang Hong fixed on the single chokepoint at Nan'an. The result: 「曶、綽承洪言，果生獲元」 — Chen Hu and Zheng Chuo followed his instructions and did take Huang Yuan alive [1].

The Xianzhu zhuan gives the sequence with a slightly different detail about the actual seizure [13]: 「三年春二月，丞相亮自成都到永安。三月，黃元進兵攻臨邛縣。遣將軍陳曶討元，元軍敗，順流下江，為其親兵所縛，生致成都，斬之。」 That is, in the third month of Zhangwu 3, Huang Yuan advanced and attacked Linqiong county; Chen Hu was sent against him; his army was defeated, he fled downstream, and was bound by his own personal soldiers and delivered alive to Chengdu, where he was beheaded. The year before, in the twelfth month of Zhangwu 2, the Xianzhu zhuan records only that 「漢嘉太守黃元聞先主疾不豫，舉兵拒守」 [8].

The two accounts do not conflict on substance — one can infer that the interception at Nan'an and the seizure by his own guards describe the same collapse, with Chen Hu's force driving Huang Yuan to the point where his escort bound him — but they differ on who is said to have taken him: Yang Hong's biography credits Chen Hu and Zheng Chuo with taking him alive, while the Xianzhu zhuan says his own soldiers bound him. I give both rather than choosing one. Either way, Liu Bei died shortly after, in the fourth month of the same year [13].

q: Which Cavalier Regular Palace Attendant of Wu got drunk and collapsed at the banquet Sun Hao held for Ding Zhong on his return from an embassy to Jin, and was beheaded in the hall on Sun Hao's orders? In which year?
reply:
**Wang Fan (王蕃), courtesy name Yongyuan (永元), of Lujiang commandery.** He served as Cavalier Regular Palace Attendant (散騎中常侍) under Sun Xiu, and in Sun Hao's early reign came back into court as Regular Palace Attendant (常侍); he was beheaded below the hall on Sun Hao's order at the great banquet Sun Hao held when Ding Zhong (丁忠) returned from his embassy to Jin. The year was **266 CE** (Wu's Ganlu 甘露 2nd year).

The relevant passage in his biography reads: 「甘露二年，丁忠使晉還，皓大會群臣，蕃沉醉頓伏。皓疑而不悅，舉蕃出外。頃之請還，酒亦不解。蕃性有威嚴，行止自若，皓大怒，呵左右於殿下斬之。衛將軍滕牧、征西將軍留平請，不能得。」[1] — In Ganlu 2, when Ding Zhong returned from his mission to Jin, Sun Hao held a grand assembly of his ministers; Wang Fan got dead drunk and collapsed. Sun Hao grew suspicious and displeased, and had him carried outside. Shortly after, Wang Fan asked to return to his seat, still not sober; being a man of dignified bearing, he behaved as usual, whereupon Sun Hao flew into a rage and ordered his attendants to behead him below the hall. The General of the Guards Teng Mu and the General of the West Liu Ping pleaded for him, but could not obtain a pardon.

The Ganlu era here is that of Wu (Sun Hao's reign); its 2nd year corresponds to 266 CE.

One point worth noting: Pei Songzhi's commentary preserves a different account. Pei cites 《江表傳》: Sun Hao, following the words of shamans and scribes, thought the Jianye palace was unlucky, went west on tour to Wuchang, still intending to move the capital, and fearing the ministers would not follow, held a great banquet and bestowed gifts on officers; there he asked Wang Fan, "In archery the chief thing is not piercing the target, for men's strength is not of the same order" (射不主皮，為力不同科), what does it mean? Wang Fan pondered without answering, and Sun Hao had him beheaded right on the hall; then going out and climbing Laishan, he had close attendants take Wang Fan's head and maul it in tiger-leaps and wolf-fights, so that the head was crushed, wishing to display his authority [21]. This differs from the main biography. Pei Songzhi himself, in his note, observes that the main biography says Ding Zhong returned from Jin and Sun Hao held the great assembly at which Wang Fan was killed, that Ding Zhong's return from the north was in the spring of that year, and that Wan Yu was not yet Chancellor (he became one only in autumn), so what 《吳錄》 says is mutually inconsistent [21]. The main text of the *Sanguozhi*, however, records the drinking-and-collapse version, and it is that text which dates the killing to Ganlu 2 (266).

q: Who had the courtesy name Wenze?
reply:
"Wenze" (文則) was the courtesy name of **two** different men in the *Sanguozhi*, so the answer depends on which one you mean.

**1. Yu Jin 于禁, Wei general.** 「于禁字文則，泰山鉅平人也。」[1] He was one of the generals Chen Shou singles out in his verdict on the five: 「太祖建茲武功，而時之良將，五子爲先。」[5] He was known for strict discipline — when the Qingzhou troops plundered as the army fell back to Wuyin, he attacked them first and only reported to Cao Cao after fortifying his camp, and Cao Cao praised him: 「將軍在亂能整，討暴堅壘，有不可動之節，雖古名將，何以加之！」[3] In the twenty-fourth year of Jian'an, Cao Cao sent him to aid Cao Ren against Guan Yu at Fan; the Han River flooded and his seven armies were lost, and he surrendered to Guan Yu while Pang De alone refused to bend. Cao Cao lamented: 「吾知禁三十年，何意臨危處難，反不如龐德邪！」[2] After Sun Quan sent him back, Emperor Wen had the surrender painted on the walls of the Gaoling mausoleum; Yu Jin saw it, 「慚恚發病薨」, and was given the posthumous name Li Hou (厲侯) [2]. Chen Shou's verdict: 「于禁最號毅重，然弗克其終。」[5]

**2. Wu Fan 吳範, Wu diviner.** 「吳範字文則，會稽上虞人也。以治曆數知風氣聞於郡中。」[10] He served Sun Quan as a prognosticator, most famously predicting the capture of Guan Yu: when Guan Yu left Maicheng, Wu Fan said 「雖去不免」, fixed the hour as the next midday, and when the time passed with no news explained 「時尚未正中也」; then, as a wind stirred the curtains, he clapped his hands: 「羽至矣。」[17] Sun Quan made him Cavalry Commandant and acting Grand Astrologer, but Wu Fan hoarded his art and would not tell Sun Quan the essentials, and 「權由是恨之」[14]. He died of illness in the fifth year of Huangwu [16], and the *Wu Lu* records that he foretold his own death day — though Pei Songzhi notes that Sun Quan was not yet emperor when Wu Fan died, so the title "Bixia" (陛下) in that account is wrong [15].

So with no further clues there are two candidates: the Wei general **Yu Jin** and the Wu diviner **Wu Fan**.

q: How did Xu Zhu realize that Xu Ta and the others were plotting to assassinate Cao Cao? And how did he deal with them?
reply:
Xu Chu didn't uncover the plot by any investigation. According to his biography in the *Wei Shu*, he turned back out of a sudden unease, and Xu Ta then betrayed himself by a change of expression.

Xu Ta and the others were soldiers who regularly attended Cao Cao, and they held off only because Xu Chu was always at his side:

「時常從士徐他等謀為逆，以褚常侍左右，憚之不敢發。伺褚休下日，他等懷刀入。褚至下捨心動，即還侍。他等不知，入帳見褚，大驚愕。他色變，褚覺之，即擊殺他等。」[1]

So the sequence was: they waited for a day when Xu Chu went off duty to rest (「休下日」), then came in with knives hidden on them; Xu Chu, on reaching his rest quarters, 「心動」 — felt uneasy — and went straight back to his post; Xu Ta and the others, not knowing he would return, entered the tent, saw him, and were badly startled; Xu Ta's face changed, Xu Chu caught it, and he killed Xu Ta and the rest on the spot. The biography records no questioning and no wider conspiracy being uncovered.

As for when: the passage sits immediately after Xu Chu's following Cao Cao against Yuan Shao at Guandu (「從討袁紹於官渡」), so it belongs to roughly that period, but the text itself only says 「時」 (at that time) and names no year.

The result was increased trust: 「太祖益親信之，出入同行，不離左右。」[1] — Cao Cao afterwards kept him in constant attendance, going in and out with him and never letting him leave his side.

Two points on the sources. First the name: the main text writes 徐他, while Pei Songzhi's note writes 徐佗 — the same man under a variant character. Second, that note is Pei Songzhi's own comment on why Xu Chu was left out of the sacrifices in Cao Cao's temple, and he cites this very incident as evidence of his loyalty: 「徐佗謀逆而許褚心動，忠誠之至遠同於日磾」[4] — comparing Xu Chu's instinctive alertness to that of Jin Midi. This is Pei Songzhi's judgement (「臣松之以為」), not a quotation from another book. Beyond the plot, the discovery and the killing, the sources give no motive for Xu Ta and no indication that anyone stood behind him.

q: What did Liu Bei say to Zhuge Liang when he entrusted his heir to him on his deathbed? How did Zhuge Liang reply? And what instructions did Liu Bei leave for the Later Sovereign?
reply:
**Short answer:** On his deathbed at Yong'an in the spring of Zhangwu 3 (223), Liu Bei told Zhuge Liang that his talent was ten times Cao Pi's and that if his heir was worth supporting, he should support him — but if the boy proved worthless, Zhuge Liang might "take it himself." Zhuge Liang wept and swore to exhaust his strength and keep faith unto death. To his heir Liu Shan, Liu Bei left both a spoken instruction to serve the Chancellor as a father and a written testament urging small virtues and hard study.

The *Zhuge Liang zhuan* records the charge itself:

「章武三年春，先主於永安病篤，召亮於成都，屬以後事，謂亮曰：『君才十倍曹丕，必能安國，終定大事。若嗣子可輔，輔之；如其不才，君可自取。』亮涕泣曰：『臣敢竭股肱之力，效忠貞之節，繼之以死！』」[1]

("In the spring of Zhangwu 3 the Former Sovereign, gravely ill at Yong'an, summoned Liang from Chengdu and entrusted him with affairs to come, saying: 'Your talent is ten times Cao Pi's; you will surely stabilize the state and in the end accomplish the great enterprise. If the heir can be supported, support him; if he has no ability, you may take it yourself.' Liang wept and said: 'I dare to exhaust the strength of my arms and legs, to render loyal and steadfast service, and to follow it with death!'")

The *Xianzhu zhuan* gives the frame: Zhuge Liang comes from Chengdu to Yong'an in the second month, then 「先主病篤，託孤於丞相亮，尚書令李嚴為副。夏四月癸巳，先主殂於永安宮，時年六十三」[22] — the dying sovereign entrusted the orphan to Chancellor Zhuge Liang with Li Yan, Prefect of the Masters of Writing, as deputy, and died in the fourth month at sixty-three. Li Yan's own biography confirms that in the third year 「先主疾病，嚴與諸葛亮並受遺詔輔少主」[24], he and Zhuge Liang jointly received the testamentary edict to assist the young lord.

The same Zhuge Liang passage continues with the words for the heir: 「先主又為詔敕後主曰：『汝與丞相從事，事之如父。』」[1] ("The Former Sovereign further issued an edict admonishing the Later Sovereign: 'Do business with the Chancellor, and serve him as you would your father.'") Pei Songzhi's note quotes the *Zhuge Liang ji* for the fuller testamentary edict: 「勿以惡小而為之，勿以善小而不為。惟賢惟德，能服於人。汝父德薄，勿效之。可讀漢書、禮記，間暇歷觀諸子及六韜、商君書，益人意智」[16] ("Do not do a small evil because it is small; do not fail to do a small good because it is small. Only worthiness and virtue can win men over. Your father was thin in virtue; do not imitate him. You may read the *Han shu* and *Li ji*, and at leisure survey the philosophers and the *Liu tao* and *Shang jun shu* — they benefit a man's mind and wisdom.") The same note adds that at the very end he called Liu Yong, Prince of Lu, and told him: 「吾亡之後，汝兄弟父事丞相，令卿與丞相共事而已」[16] — after his death the brothers were to treat the Chancellor as a father and simply work together with him.

Not everyone read the "you may take it yourself" line as noble. Pei's note cites Sun Sheng, who said of the charge 「備之命亮，亂孰甚焉」[3] — nothing could be more disorderly — arguing that a genuine trust in a loyal man needs no such words, while to the wrong man it opens the road to usurpation, and that only 「幸值劉禪闇弱，無猜險之性，諸葛威略，足以檢衛異端，故使異同之心無由自起耳」[3], Liu Shan's dullness and Zhuge Liang's prestige, kept trouble from arising. The *Yuan zi*, also quoted by Pei, praises Zhuge Liang for 「受六尺之孤，攝一國之政，事凡庸之君，專權而不失禮」[2]. Whether the offer was sincerity or a calculated bond is not something the text settles; the record simply sets the two views side by side.

q: How many different people named Zhao Da appear in the Records of the Three Kingdoms, and what did each of them do?
reply:
In the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* the name Zhao Da (赵达) appears in two contexts: a diviner of Wu, and a 校事 (secret investigator) under Cao Cao in Wei.

**Zhao Da the diviner of Wu** (in the biography of Wu Fan, Liu Dun, and Zhao Da)

He was a man of Henan who studied under the Han palace attendant Shan Fu, and, holding that "the southeast had a kingly aura" where he could escape trouble, crossed the Yangtze: 「謂東南有王者氣，可以避難，故脫身渡江」[2]. He practiced the nine-palace single-calculation art: 「治九宮一算之術，究其微旨，是以能應機立成」[2]. His feats included stating the number of beans scattered on a mat, finding a cask of wine and three catties of venison hidden by a host who claimed he had nothing to offer, and computing a number written on a slip sealed in an empty granary [2].

He guarded his method jealously: though Kan Ze and Yin Li, "famous Confucians and good men," came in person to study with him, 「達祕而不告」[1]; his long-time pupil, the Grand Astrologer's Assistant Gongsun Teng, was put off again and again, until Zhao Da pretended the manuscript had been stolen by his son-in-law — 「遂從此絕」[1]. Sun Quan had him reckon on every campaign and the results matched his words, but 「權問其法，達終不語，由此見薄，祿位不至」[4]. He foretold the exact day of his own death and died on schedule; Sun Quan sought his book, questioned his daughter, and opened the coffin, all in vain — 「法術絕焉」[4]. Pei Songzhi's note quotes the *Wu Shu*: when Sun Quan took the imperial title, Zhao Da told him he would reign twice as long as Han Gaozu's twelve years, and it proved true [5]. Pei's note quoting the *Wu Lu* counts him among Wu's "eight marvels": 「及範、惇、達八人，世皆稱妙，謂之八絕云」[7].

**Zhao Da the 校事 under Cao Cao**

When 校事 officers including Lu Hong and Zhao Da were set up to watch over the officials, Gao Rou protested: 「達等數以憎愛擅作威福，宜檢治之」[12]. Cao Cao brushed him off — 「卿知達等，恐不如吾也。要能刺舉而辨衆事，使賢人君子為之，則不能也」[12] — and only after their corruption came to light did he have them killed to apologize to Gao Rou: 「達等後姧利發，太祖殺之以謝於柔」[12]. The same name appears in Xu Miao's biography: when drink was banned and Xu Miao was drunk, the 校事 Zhao Da questioned him about official business, Xu Miao answered 「中聖人」, and Zhao Da reported it to Cao Cao, who was furious; Xu Miao escaped punishment only through Xianyu Fu's explanation [16].

The name is thus recorded in three places but in two settings — the Wu diviner, and the Wei 校事 in Gao Rou's and Xu Miao's biographies. Since both Wei passages describe a 校事 serving 太祖 (Cao Cao), 由此看 they are most likely one and the same man; the text itself does not state this outright, so two people is the reasonable count. Neither is given birth or death years: the Wu diviner's death is recorded only as falling on the day he had calculated, and the Wei officer's only as Cao Cao's executing him after his graft was exposed.
